name: Tulamben
summary: Black sand bay on Bali's northeast coast with a large shore-accessible WWII wreck and a dense concentration of macro and muck sites along the same stretch of shoreline.

highlights.label: USAT Liberty
highlights.note: Built 1918 at Hackensack NJ by Federal Shipbuilding, 411ft 6in (125m). Torpedoed 11 January 1942 by the Japanese submarine I-66 (later renumbered I-166) while running cargo from Australia to the Philippines; all 54 aboard survived. Beached off Tulamben and capsized 14 January 1942. Tremors from the 1963 Mount Agung eruption slid her off the beach into 25-100ft (7.6-30m), which is where she lies now, roughly a one-minute surface swim out. Divable from Open Water within the 18m limit, which covers most of the hull. Heavily crowded from about 09:00.

highlights.label: Macro and critter subjects
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: Tulamben is marketed almost entirely on the Liberty, but the macro diving along the same bay is why photographers stay a week. Nudibranchs, ghost pipefish, ribbon eels, scorpionfish across the wreck, the reef sites and the black sand.

highlights.label: Black volcanic sand muck sites
highlights.note: Environment, distinct from the macro subjects above. Sites east of Tulamben village (Seraya, Emerald, Alamanda) are black sand and rubble slopes rather than reef.

highlights.label: The Drop-Off
highlights.note: Sheer wall at the eastern end of the bay, deeper profile than the wreck, occasional larger pelagics.

species.name: Great barracuda
species.note: Resident individuals on and around the Liberty.

species.name: Bumphead parrotfish
species.note: Sources disagree. ZuBlu lists schooling bumpheads on the Liberty as a current feature; a later field account states the resident school disappeared during the COVID period and has not reliably returned. Encoded conservatively as unreliable in all months pending verification. Historically a dawn sighting on the wreck, and one of the two real reasons to stay locally rather than day-trip.

species.name: Ocean sunfish
species.note: Present in Bali waters during the Jul-Oct upwelling but far less reliable at Tulamben than at Nusa Penida. Do not plan a Tulamben trip around this.

species.name: Blacktip reef shark
species.note: Reported at the Drop-Off; not a reason to come.

trip_formats.note: Nearly every Tulamben site including the Liberty is a shore entry over a pebble beach. Local porters carry tanks. No boat needed.
Staying in Tulamben village or Amed gets you sunrise access to the wreck, which is the single biggest quality-of-experience variable here.

Widely sold from Sanur, Seminyak and Ubud, but it is a 3 to 3.5 hour drive each way and puts you on the wreck at peak crowding. Format mismatch risk: the day-trip product delivers a materially worse version of the site than an overnight stay.

required_certs.note: Only relevant if you are working the 28m bow repeatedly. Irrelevant for the shallow hull.

conditions.experience_note: Pebble beach entry can be awkward in swell and is the main hazard here, not depth or current. Open Water covers the majority of the Liberty; Advanced opens the 28m bow. Wreck penetration is a technical activity and is not what the standard guided dive does.

operating_note: Open year-round. Shore diving in a sheltered bay with resident operators, so there is no season closure and no fleet to reposition. Wet season (Dec-Feb) costs visibility, not access.

name: Nusa Penida
summary: Island group off southeast Bali inside a marine protected area, with a year-round reef manta population, a seasonal cold-water upwelling that brings ocean sunfish to divable depth, and healthy hard coral on the north coast.

highlights.label: Reef manta rays
highlights.note: Genuinely year-round, not seasonal, which is unusual and is the strongest single claim in this record. A six-year photo-ID study inside the MPA identified 624 individuals across Manta Bay (a foraging site, mostly juveniles and immature males) and Manta Point (a cleaning and courtship site), with an 82% resighting rate, among the highest recorded anywhere.

highlights.label: Ocean sunfish (mola)
highlights.note: Jul-Oct only, driven by Indian Ocean upwelling that pushes 16-22C water up the south and west coasts. This is the reason to come in the cold season and the reason not to expect tropical conditions.

highlights.label: North coast hard coral
highlights.note: Under-marketed relative to the two headline animals. Toyapakeh, SD, Ped and Sental carry dense, healthy hard coral in warm clear water and are what most divers actually spend their bottom time on.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Present in the MPA in every month. Manta Point sightings roughly double in May, coinciding with a courtship peak in April-May. Dec-Mar cancellations at Manta Point are caused by surface swell, not by the animals leaving.

species.name: Ocean sunfish
species.note: Best odds are roughly one sighting in three dives with an experienced guide during peak season, so budget multiple days. Crystal Bay is the most reliable site, typically at 20-30m. The Bali Ocean Sunfish Research Project cautions that the apparent seasonal peak partly tracks diver numbers rather than fish abundance, and that molas are also recorded outside the cold window.

species.name: Whitetip reef shark
species.note: Regular on the north coast sites and around Crystal Bay.

trip_formats.note: Basing on Nusa Penida or Nusa Lembongan gets you first boats to Manta Point and Crystal Bay, before the day-trip fleet arrives.
The dominant format. Fast boat from Sanur, two or three dives, back the same evening. Workable, but you arrive at the sites at peak traffic.

Format mismatch warning. The largest visitor volume at Manta Bay is snorkel tours from Bali, not divers. If you book by searching 'Nusa Penida manta' you will mostly be shown snorkel products. Manta Bay is shallow enough that snorkelling genuinely works there; Manta Point and Crystal Bay are not snorkel sites.

conditions.experience_note: Current is a condition here, not an attraction. North coast sites run as sustained drift and are manageable; Crystal Bay and Manta Point produce unpredictable down- and up-currents and are where incidents happen. Open Water is workable at Manta Point in calm conditions; 50+ logged dives is the practical bar for Crystal Bay, and Advanced is effectively required for mola dives at 30m. Thermocline drops to 16-19C during the Jul-Oct upwelling: a 3mm suit is not enough in cold season.

operating_note: No closure, but Dec-Mar brings rough surface conditions and frequent same-day cancellations at Manta Point and Crystal Bay. Operators keep running; the boats just turn back more often. Book buffer days in those months.

name: Komodo
summary: National park between Flores and Sumbawa where cold Indian Ocean water meets warm Flores Sea water through narrow channels, producing strong-current pinnacle diving in the north and cold plankton-rich manta and macro diving in the south.

highlights.label: Channel and pinnacle current diving
highlights.note: Genuinely the product here, not a hazard to tolerate. Castle Rock, Crystal Rock, Batu Bolong and The Cauldron are dived specifically because the current stacks fish on the upcurrent side. Reef hooks are standard.

highlights.label: Reef manta aggregations
highlights.note: Karang Makassar ('Manta Point') in the middle of the park and Manta Alley in the south. Feeding rather than cleaning behaviour at Manta Alley, in cold green water, which is a very different experience from the clear-water cleaning stations people picture.

highlights.label: Southern macro and critter diving
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: Komodo is sold on dragons, drift and mantas, and almost nobody books it for macro. The cold upwelling sites in the south (Cannibal Rock, Yellow Wall, Torpedo Alley) are a serious critter destination with frogfish, nudibranchs, pygmy seahorses and rhinopias.

highlights.label: Hard and soft coral cover
highlights.note: Over 260 coral species and 1,000+ fish species inside the park. Batu Bolong in particular is close to complete coral cover from 5m to past 30m.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Present year-round in the park; concentrations reported strongest Dec-Feb in the south when plankton density peaks. That is also the roughest time to reach the southern sites, which is the trade nobody mentions.

species.name: Grey reef shark
species.note: Holding in current on the northern pinnacles, particularly Castle Rock and Crystal Rock.

species.name: Pygmy seahorse
species.note: Southern sites. Guide-dependent.

trip_formats.note: The only format that reaches the southern sites (Manta Alley, Cannibal Rock, Horseshoe Bay) in reasonable time. Day boats from Labuan Bajo cannot get there and back.

Day boats from Labuan Bajo cover the central and northern park: Karang Makassar, Batu Bolong, Castle Rock, Crystal Rock, The Cauldron. Long boat days, 1.5 to 3 hours each way. Format mismatch risk: the southern macro and Manta Alley are simply not on the menu from a land base, and booking 'Komodo' from Labuan Bajo means booking the north half.
High-volume snorkel and boat-tour traffic from Labuan Bajo, mostly combining Komodo dragons with a snorkel stop at Karang Makassar. Same site as the manta dive, entirely different product and crowd.

required_certs.note: Common on liveaboards; repetitive deep pinnacle profiles.

conditions.experience_note: Two different destinations in one park. North is warm (27-28C) and clear with hard current; south runs 22-24C on upwelling with green plankton-rich water and visibility that can fall to 5m. Divers pack for Indonesia and get cold in the south. Downcurrents and washing-machine conditions occur at the pinnacles and are the real risk; reef hooks, negative entries and SMB competence are expected. Advanced is the practical floor despite some operators taking Open Water divers to the easier sites.

operating_note: The park stays open and the northern sites are diveable year-round from Labuan Bajo. The 'limited' months reflect the south: Dec-Feb monsoon swell makes the southern sites and the crossing to them unreliable, and liveaboard itineraries shift or shorten. Confusingly, Dec-Feb is also when the southern manta aggregation is strongest, so the best manta window and the worst access window overlap.

name: Raja Ampat
summary: Archipelago of roughly 1,500 islands at the centre of the Coral Triangle, holding the highest recorded reef fish and coral diversity of any marine region, dived from liveaboards and from resorts and homestays around the Dampier Strait and Misool.

highlights.label: Peak global reef biodiversity
highlights.note: The headline is usually mantas, which undersells it badly. Over 1,600 reef fish species and roughly three quarters of the world's known hard coral species. Cape Kri holds the record for the most fish species counted on a single dive at 374. If you only chase the mantas you have missed the destination.

highlights.label: Reef manta cleaning stations
highlights.note: Manta Sandy in the Dampier Strait is shallow enough at 5-8m to work as a snorkel site as well as a dive. Manta Ridge is deeper and current-swept. Oceanic mantas are a separate and much less predictable proposition at Magic Mountain in Misool.

highlights.label: Endemic and cryptic species
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: Raja Ampat has endemics you cannot see anywhere else on earth. The Raja Ampat walking shark (an epaulette shark that moves across the reef on its fins) is a night-dive target, along with tasselled wobbegongs sleeping under table coral and several pygmy seahorse species.

highlights.label: Dampier Strait current diving
highlights.note: Genuinely a draw here rather than a hazard to be managed, which is why it sits in highlights and not only in conditions. The strait funnels nutrient-rich water between islands and the sites that catch it hardest (Cape Kri, Blue Magic, Sardine Reef) are the ones with the fish density.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Resident at the cleaning stations year-round with a Dec-Apr concentration. Encounter probability at Manta Sandy in season is reported around 95%, which is unusually high for a manta site.

species.name: Giant oceanic manta ray
species.note: Magic Mountain in Misool, Dec-Mar. Reported encounter probability around 40%, so treat it as a bonus rather than an itinerary driver. Misool is a long way from the Dampier Strait resorts.

species.name: Raja Ampat walking shark
species.note: Endemic to the region. Night dives only; it walks across shallow rubble on its pectoral fins. Reported around 85% on a guided night dive. Species-level naming across sources is loose, since several Hemiscyllium species occur in the wider area.

species.name: Tasselled wobbegong
species.note: Resident, typically motionless under table corals during the day.

species.name: Pygmy seahorse
species.note: Multiple species present. Entirely guide-dependent; the sites are known to specific divemasters rather than published.

species.name: Whale shark
species.note: IMPORTANT DISAMBIGUATION. Whale sharks are widely advertised alongside Raja Ampat but they are not in Raja Ampat. The aggregation is in Cenderawasih Bay, roughly a three-day passage east, where the animals gather around fishing platforms (bagans) and are hand-fed by fishermen. Encoded 'absent' for Raja Ampat itself, and flagged as provisioned rather than natural. If whale sharks are the reason for the trip, you are booking the wrong itinerary.

trip_formats.note: The only way to reach Misool, Wayag and the northern islands in one trip. Dry-season itineraries spread across the archipelago; wet-season ones retreat to sheltered water.
Resorts cluster around the Dampier Strait and Misool. Covers the highest-density sites (Cape Kri, Blue Magic, Sardine Reef, Manta Sandy) but not the archipelago.

Village homestays are a distinct and much cheaper format, typically snorkel-oriented with limited or no tank fills and basic boats. Genuinely good value and the money stays local, but do not book one expecting a resort dive operation. Verify tank supply and boat range before committing.

required_certs.note: Standard on liveaboards; long repetitive days.

conditions.experience_note: Warm water and no thermocline, so exposure is easy, but current is the whole story. The Dampier Strait sites that make Raja Ampat famous are current-dependent and can run hard enough to require reef hooks and negative entries. Buoyancy in surging water over fragile coral is the skill that matters. Not a first tropical destination despite the benign temperatures.

operating_note: The 'limited' case this field exists for. Nothing closes, but from roughly May to September the southern monsoon brings strong winds, high waves and visibility down to 10-15m, and a substantial share of the liveaboard fleet suspends Raja Ampat itineraries or repositions elsewhere in Indonesia. July and August are the worst of it. Resorts stay open and sheltered sites stay diveable, so you can still go, at lower prices, with fewer options and a real chance of blown-out days.

name: Lembeh Strait
summary: Narrow sheltered strait of black volcanic sand between Bitung and Lembeh Island, dived almost entirely for rare and cryptic invertebrates and fish on barren sediment slopes.

highlights.label: Black sand muck environment
highlights.note: The environment, and the defining one. Barren sand and rubble slopes with almost no coral, which is precisely why the camouflaged animals are findable. Sites like Hairball, Aer Prang and Critter Hunt look like nothing until a guide stops moving. If you need scenery, this is the wrong destination.

highlights.label: Rare critter density
highlights.note: The subjects, distinct from the environment above. Hairy frogfish, flamboyant cuttlefish, Ambon scorpionfish, wonderpus, mimic octopus, blue-ringed octopus, eight-plus frogfish species. Lembeh is where several of these animals are reliably findable rather than a once-a-decade sighting.

highlights.label: Mawali wreck and jetty dives
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: Lembeh is not exclusively sand. The Mawali wreck, Police Pier, Angel's Window and Nudi Falls are structure dives with walls, seagrass and coral. Divers who assume a full week of grey sand are often relieved.

species.name: Hairy frogfish
species.note: Resident and reliably found by guides year-round. Lembeh is the single most reliable place in the world for this animal.

species.name: Mimic octopus
species.note: Resident on the open sand flats. Less reliable than the frogfish but still a realistic target on a week's diving.

species.name: Wonderpus
species.note: Resident but genuinely less frequent than the headline critters.

trip_formats.note: The only sensible format and effectively the only one offered. Dedicated critter resorts along the strait, three to four dives a day, short boat rides of 5-20 minutes. Guide quality is the single biggest variable in the entire trip, more than site choice or season.

conditions.experience_note: Technically the least demanding diving in this dataset: shallow, sheltered, minimal current, 5-30m. The real skill requirement is buoyancy discipline, because you spend the dive hovering centimetres above silt that clouds instantly and ruins the sighting for everyone behind you. Visibility is permanently poor by tropical standards and that is a feature, not a problem to solve. Cool months (Jul-Aug, 25-26C) warrant a 5mm.

operating_note: Open year-round. The strait is narrow and sheltered on both sides, so weather rarely stops diving. Jul-Aug brings cooler nutrient-rich water which lowers visibility but is reported to increase critter activity, making the 'worst' visibility months arguably the best diving months.

name: Alor
summary: Remote island group roughly 1,000km east of Bali where cold upwelling through the Pantar Strait supports pristine hard coral walls, a serious muck-diving scene, and a September to December pelagic season, with a fraction of the traffic of comparable Indonesian destinations.

highlights.label: Near-pristine coral walls
highlights.note: Over 45 dive sites carrying more than 1,000 fish species and 500 coral species, in clear water with almost no diver traffic. Alor gets a small fraction of Komodo's or Raja Ampat's numbers and the reefs show it. Visibility reaches 30-40m+ in the calm season.

highlights.label: Kalabahi and Beangabang Bay muck
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: Alor is sold as a remote pristine-reef destination and its muck sites are barely marketed at all. Rhinopias, wunderpus, mimic octopus, halimeda ghost pipefish, frogfish and pygmy seahorses on black sand inside the sheltered bays.

highlights.label: September to December pelagic season
highlights.note: Genuinely surprising for a destination nobody associates with big animals. When the cold upwelling runs hardest, hammerheads, thresher sharks and mola turn up in the Pantar Strait. Corroborated across two independent sources, though the exact windows differ and neither is research-grade. Conditions in that window are the hardest of the year.

highlights.label: Blue and sperm whale migration
highlights.note: Not encountered underwater, and the reason it is ranked fourth rather than omitted: the Pantar Strait is a deep-water migration corridor and blue and sperm whales pass through northbound June-July and southbound September-November. These are surface and boat sightings during transits between dive sites, not a dive product, and no operator sells them as one.

species.name: Scalloped hammerhead
species.note: CORROBORATION IMPROVED. Two independent sources now support a cold-upwelling hammerhead season, though they disagree on extent: ZuBlu gives March-November with Sep-Nov strongest, Alor Underwater Explorers gives a Sep-Dec pelagic season. Encoded to the overlap plus the stronger claim. Still no research literature located, so this remains a commercial-consensus claim rather than a verified one. Do not book Alor solely for this.

species.name: Thresher shark
species.note: Reported in the Sep-Dec pelagic season. Genus-level; the source does not resolve species. Occasional rather than expected, and nothing like the daily reliability at Malapascua.

species.name: Ocean sunfish
species.note: Sep-Dec with the cold water, at depth. Same upwelling mechanism as Nusa Penida but a different month window, which is worth noting for anyone assuming Indonesian mola season is a single thing.

species.name: Rhinopias
species.note: A genuine draw for photographers and one of the few places outside Ambon and Lembeh where it is a realistic target. Genus-level because sources do not resolve species.

species.name: Wonderpus
species.note: In the muck bays.

trip_formats.note: Small resorts in Kalabahi Bay. Getting there is the hard part and it is worse than it looks: fly to Jakarta or Bali, connect to Kupang in Timor, then Wings Air to Mali Airport on Alor. The onward flight usually departs early morning, so an overnight in Kupang is effectively mandatory in each direction.
Alor appears on eastern Indonesia itineraries, often combined with Flores, Solor or the Banda Sea. The only practical way to cover the outer islands.

conditions.experience_note: Operators recommend Advanced plus 30-50 logged dives for the Pantar Strait sites, which run negative entries into serious current with downcurrent potential. Surface temperature averages around 28C but dramatic thermoclines drop it to 22-24C at depth, particularly at sites like Halerman; a 5mm full suit is the standard recommendation and the cold season needs more. Remoteness is itself a risk factor, with the nearest chamber a long chain of flights away.

operating_note: Dec-Mar is the rainy season: visibility drops and some resorts reduce or suspend operations, though there is no formal closure. Apr-Aug is the calm high season with 30-40m+ visibility, best for photographers and first-timers. Sep-Dec is the pelagic season with stronger currents and colder water. The two 'best' windows serve different divers, which is the useful thing to know.

name: Tubbataha Reefs
summary: Two uninhabited atolls and a separate reef in the middle of the Sulu Sea, inside a 96,828-hectare no-take national park, accessible by liveaboard for roughly three months a year.

highlights.label: Intact atoll reef system
highlights.note: The actual draw, and the thing that gets buried under shark marketing. Over 360 coral species, close to 90% of all coral species recorded in the Philippines, on reefs that have never been fished or settled. Vast staghorn fields and near-total coral cover on the walls.

highlights.label: Whitetip reef shark density
highlights.note: UNESCO records the highest known population densities of whitetip reef sharks anywhere in the world. A specific, verifiable superlative rather than the usual 'shark diving' claim.

highlights.label: Atoll walls
highlights.note: Southwest Wall, Black Rock, Ko-ok. Vertical drops from the reef crest into open Sulu Sea, dived as drifts.

highlights.label: Schooling fish and pelagics
highlights.note: Dense jack, barracuda and snapper schools, yellowfin tuna, plus mantas and occasional whale sharks off the walls.

species.name: Whitetip reef shark
species.note: Highest known population density in the world per UNESCO. Resident; you simply cannot get there for nine months of the year.

species.name: Green turtle
species.note: The atolls are a significant nesting, resting and juvenile development area, so densities are unusually high.

species.name: Napoleon wrasse
species.note: Endangered elsewhere in the region and heavily fished; Tubbataha holds a protected population. UNESCO names it explicitly, but only that one source does, so this sits at medium rather than high despite the source being tier 1.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Present but not a cleaning-station product. No reliable aggregation site inside the park.

species.name: Whale shark
species.note: Recorded in the park but not predictable on a given trip. Encoded as unreliable in all months rather than assigned a season no source supports.

trip_formats.note: The only access, and only during the season. Roughly 10-12 hours crossing from Puerto Princesa, Palawan, which is a 90-minute flight from Manila. No land base exists; the park has a ranger station and nothing else. Park entry fees are charged per diver.

required_certs.note: Repeated wall dives across a week.

conditions.experience_note: Current is the variable that matters and it is tidal rather than constant; operators time dives around slack. When it runs on the wall corners it runs hard, and there is nothing downstream but open Sulu Sea, so SMB competence is not optional. Visibility is consistently excellent, which makes the currents easier to read than at somewhere like Komodo.

operating_note: The hardest access window in this dataset. Roughly mid-March to mid-June only, which is why March and June read 'limited' rather than 'open'. Outside it the northeast monsoon (Nov-Mar) and southwest monsoon (Jul-Oct) make the crossing to an exposed mid-sea atoll unsafe. Nothing about the reef changes; you simply cannot get there. Boats sell out 9-12 months ahead as a direct result.

name: Malapascua
summary: Small island off northern Cebu with a seamount cleaning station where pelagic thresher sharks are seen at dawn effectively every day of the year, plus a dense and largely unadvertised macro scene on the surrounding reefs.

highlights.label: Pelagic thresher sharks
highlights.note: The only destination where pelagic threshers are seen predictably and daily. They come to reef-fish cleaning stations on a seamount plateau; a PLOS ONE study documented 97 cleaning events over 1,230 hours of video across 232 days, with frequency highest in the morning and declining through the day. Dawn departures around 04:00, no strobes or lights permitted.

highlights.label: Macro and critter subjects
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: Malapascua is sold entirely on threshers, and almost every diver books two or three nights around one dawn dive. The macro on the surrounding reefs is competitive with dedicated Philippine critter destinations. Multiple pygmy seahorse species, flamboyant cuttlefish, blue-ringed octopus, frogfish, ghost pipefish, extensive nudibranch diversity.

highlights.label: Gato Island
highlights.note: Cavern swim-through under the island plus a wall known locally as 'Nudibranch City'. Sea snakes, sleeping whitetip reef sharks, pygmy seahorses. Roughly a 45-minute boat ride.

highlights.label: Mandarinfish courtship at Lighthouse
highlights.note: Dusk dive on a shallow rubble site; red focus lights only. Stationary and shallow, which suits it to divers who are not comfortable with the dawn seamount dive.

species.name: Pelagic thresher shark
species.note: Present year-round; the constraint is time of day, not month. Cleaning-station visits decline significantly from morning to evening. Sighting probability on a given dawn dive is high but not guaranteed, and surface conditions cancel more dives Jun-Oct than the sharks do.

species.name: Mandarinfish
species.note: Courtship display at sunset, roughly a 20-minute window. Reliable to the point of being scheduled.

species.name: Flamboyant cuttlefish
species.note: Chocolate Island is the most consistent site. One field account reports a mating-season concentration in roughly late April to May; this is a single observation and the encoded peak is weakly supported.

species.name: Pygmy seahorse
species.note: Multiple pygmy species reported around Gato Island and the surrounding sites. Species-level identification in the sources is loose; H. bargibanti is the one consistently named.

species.name: Whitetip reef shark
species.note: Resting in the Gato Island cavern during the day.

trip_formats.note: The only sensible format. Getting there is a flight to Cebu, roughly 3.5 hours by road to Maya Port, then a short ferry, so budget a full travel day each way. Dawn thresher dive plus two or three day dives is the standard rhythm.
Some Visayas liveaboard itineraries call at Monad Shoal, usually for a single dawn dive. Lower odds than a multi-day land stay, since you get one attempt rather than three or four.

required_certs.note: Consecutive deep dawn dives on the shoal stack up nitrogen fast.

conditions.experience_note: SHIPPING CONTESTED. Inshore sites are calm and beginner-friendly; the seamounts carry moderate to strong current. Four sources give four different answers on where the thresher dive actually happens and how deep, which is what drives the certification gate: the PLOS ONE study puts the cleaning stations on the Monad Shoal plateau at 15-25m; DAN says the sharks relocated to Kimud Shoal at 12-15m; ZuBlu says Monad is 30m+ with Kimud only slightly shallower, and that Open Water divers may be admissible alongside an instructor; Divernet describes divers holding 12-14m at Kimud for up to 80 minutes. Encoded as Advanced because under-gating is the dangerous direction of error. Confirm the shoal and depth with your operator at booking. Repeated deep dawn dives on consecutive days make nitrox worthwhile. No lights or strobes on the shark dive.

operating_note: No formal closure. Typhoon risk runs roughly May-Oct and sources disagree on how badly it bites: DAN says avoid Jun-Sep, Divernet calls Mar-Sep the most stable window, and one field account calls the Jul-Dec rainy season mild. Encoded 'limited' across the contested span rather than picking a side. See OQ-07.

name: Anilao
summary: Stretch of coastline three hours south of Manila with a dense concentration of macro and muck sites in a small area, plus one of the more established blackwater diving operations in Asia.

highlights.label: Nudibranch and critter density
highlights.note: Widely described as the nudibranch capital of the world, with roughly 100 species realistically achievable in a single week. The claim is repeated across sources without a survey behind it, so treat the superlative as marketing and the density as real.

highlights.label: Blackwater diving
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: Anilao is booked almost entirely as a macro-photography destination and its blackwater diving is under-known outside that circle. Larval-stage fish, cephalopods and gelatinous animals, a proportion of which are undescribed. Alongside Kona, one of very few places running blackwater as a routine scheduled product.

highlights.label: Muck sites
highlights.note: Environment, distinct from the macro subjects. Secret Bay and similar sand and rubble sites, alongside genuine coral reef at Twin Rocks and Beatrice. Anilao mixes both within a short boat ride, which is unusual.

highlights.label: Wide-angle reef sites
highlights.note: Twin Rocks, Beatrice and Mainit Point carry healthy coral, schooling fish, occasional barracuda and large trevally. Anilao is not exclusively a macro destination, though it is sold as one.

species.name: Bobbit worm
species.note: Night dives on the sand sites.

species.name: Frogfish
species.note: Multiple species. Sources do not resolve to species level, so this entry is deliberately genus-level rather than falsely precise.

species.name: Ghost pipefish
species.note: Genus-level; multiple species reported. Corroborated across both sources.

trip_formats.note: Dive resorts along the coast running small bangka boats, typically four divers maximum, with very short transits. Three to four dives a day plus optional night and blackwater.
Roughly three hours by road from Manila, which makes Anilao the standard weekend destination for Manila-based divers. Workable, but blackwater and night diving effectively require an overnight stay.

conditions.experience_note: Muck sites are shallow and current-free and suit any certification level. The wide-angle points (Beatrice, Mainit) carry real current and are a step up. Blackwater is the exception: open water at night with no bottom reference, run on a tether, and gated by operator judgement rather than by card. Buoyancy over silt is the skill that determines whether your guide can show you anything. Second source gives depth 1-30m and notes bangka dives regularly running past 60 minutes, and recommends a 5mm minimum despite the tropical latitude.

operating_note: Season runs roughly October to May, with November and May singled out as the best months by both sources. Jun-Sep is the southwest monsoon and typhoon window: resorts stay open and diving continues on calm days, but sea state and rain cancel dives and photography groups avoid it. Encoded 'limited' rather than 'closed' because access never actually stops.

name: Moalboal
summary: Village on the west coast of Cebu with a permanent multi-million sardine school holding metres from shore in shallow water, plus a wall island and near-guaranteed turtle sites.

highlights.label: Resident sardine school
highlights.note: Millions of Sardinella lemuru that arrived around 2012 and never left. Unlike South Africa's sardine run this has no season at all: it is 3-10 metres from the Panagsama shoreline at 5-15m depth, every day. That combination of scale, reliability and accessibility does not exist anywhere else.

highlights.label: Pescador Island
highlights.note: Wall dropping past 40m with soft coral and sea fans, plus the Cathedral Cave swim-through. Roughly 15 minutes by boat.

highlights.label: Turtle sites at Tongo Point
highlights.note: Under-marketed relative to the sardines. Tongo Point and the Tuble marine sanctuary offer close to guaranteed green turtle encounters in shallow water, which for many divers ends up being the trip highlight.

highlights.label: Shore-accessible walls
highlights.note: Corroborated by the second source and easy to miss: the coral wall starts literally metres from the Panagsama shoreline and drops past 35m. Very few destinations put wall diving within swimming distance of a beach bar.

species.name: Bali sardinella
species.note: Genuinely aseasonal and genuinely resident since roughly 2012. The one destination in this dataset where 'any month works' is the whole point rather than a hedge.

species.name: Green turtle
species.note: Near-guaranteed at Tongo Point and on the Panagsama house reef.

species.name: Pelagic thresher shark
species.note: Occasionally seen at Pescador Island, described explicitly as luck rather than a product. If threshers are the goal, Malapascua on the other side of Cebu is the destination; do not confuse the two.

species.name: Hawksbill turtle
species.note: Less common than greens here.

trip_formats.note: The sardine school is a shore entry from Panagsama beach. No boat required, which is close to unique for an attraction of this scale.
Dive shops along Panagsama running short boat trips to Pescador and Tongo Point plus unlimited house-reef access.

Format note, and here the snorkel option is genuinely competitive rather than a downgrade. The school sits at 5-15m within swimming distance of the beach, so freedivers and snorkellers get a comparable experience for the price of an environmental fee. Scuba buys you time and predator activity, not access.

conditions.experience_note: One of the easiest destinations in this dataset. The sardines are shallow, sheltered and shore-accessible; Pescador's wall goes deep but is dived shallow by most. Early morning (06:00-09:00) gives the calmest water and the most surface-active school. Environmental user fees apply.

operating_note: No closure. Both sources put the optimal window at roughly November/December to May; Jun-Aug stays good with fewer people; Sep-Nov drops in visibility and carries typhoon risk, which is why those months read 'limited'. The sardines are there regardless.

name: Socorro (Revillagigedo)
summary: Volcanic archipelago roughly 400km off Baja California, reachable only by liveaboard, with one of the largest known giant oceanic manta aggregations, up to twenty shark species, and a wintering humpback population.

highlights.label: Giant oceanic manta rays
highlights.note: Aggregate here in some of the largest numbers known anywhere, including a melanistic all-black morph. These animals routinely approach and stay with divers, which is behaviourally unusual and is the actual reason people pay for this trip. Clarion angelfish, a local endemic, clean them.

highlights.label: Multi-species shark aggregation
highlights.note: Up to twenty shark species recorded in the park. Silvertip, Galapagos, silky, whitetip reef and scalloped hammerhead are the ones divers see; tiger sharks turn up at Cabo Pearce with luck.

highlights.label: Humpback whales and bottlenose dolphins
highlights.note: Up to 2,000 humpbacks pass through, with song audible underwater through the winter months. Resident bottlenose dolphins initiate interaction with divers at Cabo Pearce and Roca Partida, which is rare behaviour and under-advertised relative to the mantas.

highlights.label: Endemic reef fish
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline. At least ten reef fish species are endemic or near-endemic, most visibly the Clarion angelfish. Nobody crosses 400km of open ocean for a 20cm angelfish, but it is the thing you cannot see anywhere else, and it is what is cleaning the mantas you came for.

species.name: Giant oceanic manta ray
species.note: Resident. Aggregates here in some of the largest numbers known anywhere. Present in every month; you can only reach the islands Nov-May.

species.name: Humpback whale
species.note: Song is audible on most dives Jan-Mar; visual underwater encounters are opportunistic and not the basis for booking. Cows with calves are present in this window.

species.name: Bottlenose dolphin
species.note: Resident pods that approach divers deliberately, most consistently at Cabo Pearce and Roca Partida.

species.name: Scalloped hammerhead
species.note: Present year-round with reported increases in the cooler Feb-Apr window. Schooling behaviour here is less consistent than at Cocos or Galapagos.

species.name: Silvertip shark
species.note: Resident year-round, particularly at Roca Partida.

species.name: Whale shark
species.note: Sources contradict each other on the window: Nov-Dec, Apr-May, or both. CONANP does not list whale shark among the park's representative species at all, which is itself a signal. Encoded as the conservative union of all claimed windows. Do not book around this. See OQ-05.

trip_formats.note: The only way to dive here. Roughly 20-30 hours of open-ocean crossing each way from Cabo San Lucas or San José del Cabo, leaving about 5 dive days with 3-4 dives daily. Book 9-12 months out for the whale window. Park fees are additional and substantial.

required_certs.note: Effectively expected by operators. 3-4 deep dives a day for five days.

conditions.experience_note: Ripping current, strong surge, negative entries, blue-water safety stops with no reference, and a two-day boat ride from any hyperbaric chamber. Operators generally require Advanced plus 50-100 logged dives, and nitrox is effectively expected. Water drops to 21-23C in the Feb-Apr whale window, which surprises people who packed for Mexico. This is not a first liveaboard. Park fee is $3,760 MXN per diver per day, charged on top of the boat, and diving hours are restricted to 07:00-18:00 by the park authority.

operating_note: RESOLVED BY TIER 1. CONANP, the Mexican protected-areas authority, states the tourist diving season as November to June, 07:00-18:00, with a park fee of $3,760 MXN per person per day. That corrects the commercial sources, which variously gave Nov-May and Nov-Jun/Jul. Encoded Nov-Jun open, Jul-Oct closed. The closure is operational and regulatory, not biological: mantas, silvertips and dolphins are resident through it.

name: Cabo Pulmo
summary: Small no-take marine park on the east cape of Baja holding the only living coral reef in the Gulf of California, and the most documented case of fish biomass recovery inside a protected area anywhere.

highlights.label: Recovered reef and fish biomass
highlights.note: The actual story, and the one that gets skipped. The reef was fished out before 1995 protection; research covering 1999-2009 documented a 463% increase in total fish biomass with top predators up roughly elevenfold, the largest recovery measured in any marine reserve anywhere. Now a UNESCO World Heritage site and the only living coral reef in the Gulf of California, built on 11 hard coral species roughly 20,000 years old. What you are diving is not a pristine reef but a rebuilt one, which is arguably more interesting.

highlights.label: Jack schools and big-fish aggregations
highlights.note: Dense tornado schools of bigeye jack, plus grouper and snapper aggregations that exist here specifically because nobody is allowed to fish them. The visual density is the direct product of the protection.

highlights.label: Bull sharks at El Vencedor
highlights.note: CONTRADICTION. Reliable at the El Vencedor wreck, but the two sources disagree sharply on when: ZuBlu gives a Feb-Jun peak, Divearoo gives bull sharks year-round with peak reliability Aug-Dec. Encoded as present year-round with no confident peak. Unbaited either way, which distinguishes this from the Playa del Carmen bull shark season on the other side of Mexico. See OQ-30.

highlights.label: El Vencedor
highlights.note: Small wreck acting as the reliable structure for the bull shark encounters.

species.name: Bull shark
species.note: Sources contradict: ZuBlu gives Feb-Jun peak, Divearoo gives year-round with Aug-Dec most reliable. Encoded flat rather than picking a side. Unbaited. See OQ-30.

species.name: Bigeye jack
species.note: Schooling year-round; the signature Cabo Pulmo image.

species.name: California sea lion
species.note: Present, though the dedicated sea lion colony diving in this region is at Los Islotes near La Paz rather than here.

species.name: Mobula ray
species.note: Present in the Gulf; the large aggregations and breaching behaviour are a La Paz product rather than a Cabo Pulmo one. Sources do not give a Cabo Pulmo-specific season.

species.name: Whale shark
species.note: Occasional in winter months. The reliable Gulf of California whale shark product is in La Paz bay, and it is a snorkel activity.

species.name: Humpback whale
species.note: Jan-Mar in the Gulf. Surface and acoustic, not an in-water product.

trip_formats.note: Small village operations. Sites are under 10 minutes from shore, so boat time is minimal. Permits are capped at roughly two dive groups per site per day, which keeps sites uncrowded but means booking ahead matters.
Commonly sold as a day trip from Cabo San Lucas or San José del Cabo, roughly two hours by road each way on partly unpaved road.
Appears on Sea of Cortez itineraries, usually combined with La Paz and the northern islands.

conditions.experience_note: Shallow reefs at 15m suit beginners; the seamounts (El Bajo, Meros) and the standard drift profile suit intermediate and up. Water hits 18C around March, which catches people who booked Mexico expecting warm water. Park rules are strict and enforced: 45-minute maximum dive time, no touching, 2m standoff from the reef, no collecting. The time limit in particular changes how you plan a dive. Access to El Vencedor runs through a weekly lottery among operators with no way to buy priority, so the headline site is not guaranteed even on a booked trip. Nearest hyperbaric chamber is San Jose del Cabo, 1.5 hours away, and the village is off-grid.

operating_note: Year-round diving with no closure. The constraint is permit capacity: roughly two dive groups per site per day, with El Vencedor allocated by weekly lottery. Both sources agree Aug-Dec gives the warmest water (27-30C) and best visibility (24-27m); ZuBlu's Feb-Jun bull shark window sits in the coldest, murkiest part of the year, which is part of why the contradiction matters. Book 3-6 months ahead for peak season.

name: Cozumel
summary: Island off the Yucatán coast on the western edge of the Mesoamerican reef, dived almost entirely as effortless north-flowing drift along a series of coral walls and swim-through systems.

highlights.label: North-flowing wall drift
highlights.note: Genuinely the product, not a hazard. The North Equatorial Current runs consistently south to north along the island's west coast and the dive plan is to descend and be carried. Almost no finning. This is what makes Cozumel workable for low-experience divers despite being wall diving.

highlights.label: Palancar, Santa Rosa and Columbia walls
highlights.note: Coral buttresses on the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, cut by tunnels and swim-throughs rather than forming a single flat face. Punta Sur's Cathedral is the well-known light-shaft swim-through; Devil's Throat below it is an advanced-only tunnel descent to around 40m and a genuine step up from everything else on the island.

highlights.label: Splendid toadfish
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline. Cozumel is booked as easy Caribbean drift diving, and almost nobody arrives knowing it has an endemic fish. Sanopus splendidus lives only here, hides under ledges, and is the one animal on the island you cannot see anywhere else on earth.

highlights.label: C-53 Felipe Xicoténcatl
highlights.note: Former US minesweeper sunk as an artificial reef, shallow and penetrable, used mainly as a training and second-dive site.

species.name: Splendid toadfish
species.note: Endemic to Cozumel and found nowhere else. Under ledges and coral overhangs; entirely guide-dependent to find.

species.name: Spotted eagle ray
species.note: Present year-round with both sources reporting more activity in winter months.

species.name: Nurse shark
species.note: Resting under ledges. Unbaited here, unlike some Caribbean nurse shark products.

trip_formats.note: Overwhelmingly the format. Two-tank morning boat with early pickups, back by early afternoon. Very large operator market, wide quality range.
Shore entries exist along the western hotel strip but are shallow rubble and nothing like the wall diving. Not why you come.

Format mismatch warning. Cozumel is a major cruise port and a very large share of in-water activity is cruise-passenger snorkel excursions on the shallow inshore reefs. These are a different set of sites from the wall diving and searching 'Cozumel reef' surfaces mostly the snorkel product.

required_certs.note: Not formally required, but Devil's Throat at Punta Sur is a multi-level tunnel descent to around 40m that both sources flag as advanced-only, and operators gate it on logged experience.

conditions.experience_note: Among the easiest wall diving anywhere: warm, clear, and the current does the work. The catch is that drift diving means you surface away from where you descended and boats follow bubbles, so SMB use and staying with the group matter more than usual. Current occasionally runs hard enough to make the deeper southern sites advanced-only. National marine park rules prohibit gloves and touching.

operating_note: Year-round diving. Both sources put the best window at roughly November to May, with February singled out for 82F water and 30m+ visibility. Aug-Oct is the peak of Caribbean hurricane season and individual days or whole weeks get cancelled, which is why those read 'limited'.

name: Yucatán Cenotes
summary: Flooded limestone sinkholes and cave systems inland of Tulum and Playa del Carmen, dived in freshwater for light, geology and haloclines rather than for marine life.

highlights.label: Cavern systems
highlights.note: Dos Ojos, Chac Mool, Tajma Ha, Carwash. Decorated limestone with stalactites and stalagmites, dived inside the daylight zone with a guide and a continuous line to open water. Visibility routinely reported around 100m because it is filtered groundwater with no particulate.

highlights.label: Haloclines and the hydrogen sulphide layer
highlights.note: The genuinely strange part, and under-described in most marketing. Where fresh groundwater floats on salt water the boundary shimmers like a mirage and refracts everything; Chac Mool and The Pit both have pronounced haloclines, The Pit's at around 13m. At Angelita and The Pit a hydrogen sulphide cloud sits at about 30m looking like a solid riverbed. Penetrating the H2S layer drops visibility to zero and leaves the smell on your gear for days. These are optical and chemical phenomena, not scenery.

highlights.label: Freshwater environment
highlights.note: Effectively no marine life, which is the point. Some small freshwater fish and bats at the entrances. Divers arriving from a reef trip should understand this is a geology and light experience, not a wildlife one.

highlights.label: Full cave systems
highlights.note: Beyond the daylight zone lie some of the longest underwater cave systems on earth. Entirely separate activity requiring full cave certification, separate operators and separate gear. Do not assume a cenote booking includes this.

species.name: Blind cave fish
species.note: Endemic troglobitic species in the Yucatán aquifer. Present but very rarely observed on recreational cavern dives, hence 'off' throughout rather than a false 'peak'. Not sourced to the guide used for the rest of this record; treat with caution.

species.name: Morelet's crocodile
species.note: Resolves the previous unsourced placeholder. Present in the surface lagoons at Casa Cenote and Carwash, described as shy and federally protected. Genuinely the most notable animal in the system and absent from most cenote marketing.

species.name: Great barracuda
species.note: In the brackish zones at Casa Cenote where the system meets the sea.

trip_formats.note: Two-tank guided cavern day from Tulum, Playa del Carmen or Cancún. Sites are inland by road; there is no boat. Guide ratios are small and mandatory.

Format mismatch warning, and a large one. The cenote market is dominated by high-volume snorkel and swim tours at the shallow open cenotes, which is an entirely different product from guided cavern diving. Searching 'cenote' returns mostly the swim tours.
Dedicated cave-diving operators in Tulum run multi-day programmes for certified cave divers, including training. This is a separate sport from the cavern day trip above.

required_certs.note: The case this field exists for. Guided cavern dives accept Open Water divers with a cavern-certified guide at Dos Ojos, Casa Cenote, Chac Mool, Carwash and Eden; the guide holds the certification and the line. The Pit and Angelita are gated on Advanced for depth (40m max). Guide ratio is capped at 4 divers per cavern guide.
Full cave certification (TDI or NSS-CDS) is mandatory beyond the daylight zone and for sites like Dreamgate. Non-negotiable and enforced. Cavern training does not grant it.

conditions.experience_note: No current, no swell, no depth pressure on most cavern routes, and constant 24-25C. The risk is entirely overhead environment: there is no direct ascent to the surface, so gas management by thirds, a primary light, a modified frog kick to avoid silting, and keeping natural daylight in sight are the rules that matter. Buoyancy failures silt out a passage for everyone behind you. 5mm minimum; freshwater at 24C over two dives is colder than it sounds. Entrance fees of MXN 250-700 are charged per cenote on top of the dive package. Maya human remains and pottery dated 9,000-13,000 years old are present in several systems and are federally protected: do not touch anything.

operating_note: Open year-round; the cenotes are inland, sheltered and thermally constant at 24-25C, so they are the reliable fallback when Caribbean weather cancels the boats. Heavy rain in the Jun-Oct wet season pushes tannins and particulate into some systems and temporarily reduces visibility; hurricanes close roads rather than sites.

name: Cocos Island
summary: Uninhabited island 550km off the Pacific coast of Costa Rica, reachable only by a 36-hour liveaboard crossing, dived almost exclusively for schooling scalloped hammerheads at seamount cleaning stations.

highlights.label: Schooling scalloped hammerheads
highlights.note: The reason the trip exists. Cleaning stations at Alcyone, Dirty Rock and Manuelita hold schools that can run to hundreds of animals overhead. You hold position behind rock in current and wait rather than swim at them.

highlights.label: Multi-species shark diversity
highlights.note: Beyond the hammerheads: whitetip reef sharks in numbers that support a well-known night feeding behaviour at Manuelita, plus Galapagos, silky, blacktip and tiger sharks.

highlights.label: Rays and large schooling fish
highlights.note: Under-advertised relative to the hammerheads. Marbled rays in aggregations, eagle rays, mantas, plus dense schools of jacks and giant trevally. Several divers report the marbled ray fields as the more memorable dive.

species.name: Scalloped hammerhead
species.note: Present year-round; schooling behaviour peaks in the Jun-Oct rainy season, which is also when visibility is at its worst. That trade-off is the central booking decision for Cocos and most operators do not spell it out.

species.name: Whitetip reef shark
species.note: Very high densities. The Manuelita night dive, where dozens hunt cooperatively across the reef, is a signature Cocos dive and does not depend on season.

species.name: Whale shark
species.note: Reported alongside the rainy-season hammerhead peak. Occasional rather than expected.

species.name: Tiger shark
species.note: Regular at Manuelita Channel in recent years. Unbaited, unlike Tiger Beach.

species.name: Marbled ray
species.note: Aggregations on sand between the pinnacles.

trip_formats.note: The only access. 36 hours each way from Puntarenas, so a 10-day trip yields roughly 7 dive days. No land facilities, no shore access, no snorkel product. Park fees are charged separately and are significant.

required_certs.note: Recommended by operators; repeated deep dives over consecutive days.

conditions.experience_note: Strong current and significant surge are the norm, not the exception. Operators expect solid buoyancy and the ability to deploy an SMB independently, because blue-water ascents away from the pinnacle are routine. Deep sites past 30m. Thermoclines are sharp and seasonal, and the cold water is often exactly where the hammerheads are. Two days from the nearest chamber.

operating_note: Liveaboards run year-round; there is no closed season. The seasonal split is a quality trade rather than an access one: Jun-Oct rainy season gives the best hammerhead schooling and the worst visibility (9-20m), Dec-May dry season gives up to 30m visibility and less consistent schooling.

name: Galápagos
summary: Volcanic archipelago on the equator where the cold Humboldt and Cromwell currents meet warm tropical water, producing large-animal diving in cold green water alongside endemic species found nowhere else.

highlights.label: Schooling scalloped hammerheads at Darwin and Wolf
highlights.note: Schools that can run over 100 animals circling the northern seamounts. Reaching Darwin and Wolf requires a liveaboard; they are far north of the inhabited islands and are not accessible on a day trip from Santa Cruz.

highlights.label: Pregnant whale sharks
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline, and a genuinely unique claim. Unlike every other whale shark aggregation on earth, which is dominated by immature males, the Galápagos animals are overwhelmingly large mature females with distended abdomens consistent with advanced pregnancy. The Galápagos Whale Shark Project was founded in 2011 specifically to study this. Nowhere else offers it.

highlights.label: Endemic cold-water species on the equator
highlights.note: Under-marketed relative to the sharks. Marine iguanas grazing algae underwater, Galápagos penguins, flightless cormorants and Galápagos fur seals, all at 0 degrees latitude. These are central-island dives, not Darwin and Wolf, and a shark-focused itinerary can skip them entirely.

highlights.label: Elasmobranch diversity
highlights.note: At least 58 elasmobranch species including 33 sharks, one of which (Bythaelurus giddingsi, a deepwater catshark) was described from Galápagos specimens in 2012.

species.name: Scalloped hammerhead
species.note: Present year-round at Darwin and Wolf. Schooling behaviour is reported strongest in the warm season (Dec-May); the reason for the aggregation is still debated in the literature. Note this cuts against the common assumption that the cold season is uniformly better for big animals.

species.name: Whale shark
species.note: Jun-Sep per Galapagos Conservation Trust, Jul-Oct per liveaboard sources; encoded as the union with Jul-Oct as peak. Almost exclusively at Darwin. Mature pregnant females, unlike every other known aggregation.

species.name: Galápagos sea lion
species.note: Endemic. Actively interactive with divers, particularly juveniles, and reported as more playful in the warm season.

species.name: Marine iguana
species.note: The only marine lizard on earth. Grazes algae underwater at shallow central-island sites; reported as more active in the warm season when the water is less punishing for a cold-blooded animal.

species.name: Ocean sunfish
species.note: Associated with the cold-season upwelling. Occasional rather than expected.

trip_formats.note: The only way to dive Darwin and Wolf, which is what most people mean by Galápagos diving. A limited number of dive liveaboard permits exist and high-season trips fill roughly 12 months ahead. National park entrance fee is charged on top.

Format mismatch warning, and an expensive one. Day boats from Puerto Ayora on Santa Cruz reach central sites like Gordon Rocks, Seymour and Floreana. These are good dives with sharks, rays and sea lions, but they are NOT Darwin and Wolf, and no day operation reaches them. Divers regularly book a land-based Galápagos trip expecting the hammerhead walls they saw in a documentary.
Large snorkel and wildlife-cruise market overlapping the same central sites. Sea lions, turtles and penguins snorkel well; the shark diving does not.

required_certs.note: Standard on dive liveaboards.
Not required, but cold-season water at 16-18C over multiple daily dives defeats most wetsuits. Many repeat visitors bring one.

conditions.experience_note: Cold, surgy and current-swept, and nothing about it resembles tropical diving. Cool season (Jun-Nov) drops to 16-18C with sharp thermoclines, strong current and rougher surface conditions; a 7mm with hood and gloves is the working minimum. Darwin and Wolf are negative-entry drift dives where you hook or hold onto rock in current and watch. Operators expect substantial logged experience. Visibility is routinely 10-15m in the productive season, so the animals arrive out of green water at close range.

operating_note: Open year-round with no closure; the split is a quality trade, not an access one. Cool season (Jun-Nov) means whale sharks, big-animal density, cold water and rough seas. Warm season (Dec-May) means calmer water, better visibility, more hammerhead schooling and more comfortable diving. Liveaboard permits are capped, so availability rather than weather is the practical constraint.

name: Kona
summary: Leeward coast of Hawai'i Island with steep volcanic drop-offs close to shore, a long-studied resident reef manta aggregation fed by nightly dive lights, open-ocean blackwater diving, and the highest rate of marine endemism of any reef system.

highlights.label: Manta ray night dive
highlights.note: Divers and snorkellers sit around downward-facing lights that concentrate zooplankton; mantas barrel-roll through the column. Two sites: Garden Eel Cove north of the airport, and Keauhou to the south. A 13-year citizen-science dataset logged over 23,000 sightings of 167 individuals across the two.

highlights.label: Blackwater diving ('Pelagic Magic')
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: Kona is where recreational blackwater diving was commercialised, and it remains one of the few places running it as a scheduled charter rather than a special request. Divers are tethered over deep open water at night to intercept the vertical migration. Almost invisible outside underwater-photography circles.

highlights.label: Endemic reef fish
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline. Hawai'i has the world's highest rate of endemism for reef fish and invertebrates; roughly a fifth to a quarter of the reef fish you see exist nowhere else. Kona is the only place to see a male flame wrasse displaying. Nobody books Kona for this and it is arguably the most distinctive thing about the diving.

highlights.label: Lava tubes, arches and caverns
highlights.note: Volcanic topography rather than coral structure. Cavern-grade rather than true cave; surge is the limiting factor on the shallower ones.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Aggregation size tracks zooplankton density rather than a calendar season, so 'year-round' is accurate but night-to-night counts swing widely, from one animal to thirty-plus. Keauhou is used predominantly by females with high site fidelity; Garden Eel Cove holds the larger aggregations. Not guaranteed on any given night.

species.name: Humpback whale
species.note: Roughly half the North Pacific population winters in Hawaiian waters. For divers this is an acoustic experience: song is audible on almost every dive in season. In-water approach is federally regulated and this is not a dive-with-whales destination. Do not book Kona in winter expecting an encounter.

species.name: Green sea turtle
species.note: Turtle Pinnacle is a cleaning station and the most consistent site.

species.name: Flame wrasse
species.note: Hawaiian endemic. Males display on deeper rubble slopes. The single best example of what Kona offers that no other destination can.

species.name: Spinner dolphin
species.note: Resident pods rest in leeward bays during the day. Encounters are typically from the boat or in passing, not sustained. Approach is federally restricted; confirm current rules with the operator.

trip_formats.note: Standard two-tank morning boat plus an optional manta night dive. Boat rides are short, 20-45 minutes, with small groups.
Multiple viable shore entries along the Kona coast. Summer swell is lower, which is the main constraint.

Format mismatch warning. The manta night is sold in two distinct products at very different prices: a scuba dive where you kneel on the bottom, and a much higher-volume surface snorkel where you hold a floating light board. Searching 'Kona manta ray dive' returns mostly the snorkel product. The animal experience is comparable; the price and the crowd are not.

conditions.experience_note: Among the least demanding conditions in this dataset: minimal current, warm water, short boat rides, diveable most days of the year. Blackwater is the exception and requires comfort with no bottom reference, no visual horizon and a tether, and operators gate it on experience rather than card level. Winter swell restricts shore entries.

operating_note: Leeward coast, sheltered by the volcano. Diveable close to every day of the year. Winter swell restricts shore entries but not boat operations.

name: Silfra
summary: Freshwater rift fissure in a national park, filled with filtered glacial meltwater at 2-4C year-round, dived for extreme visibility and the tectonic setting rather than for marine life.

highlights.label: Mid-Atlantic rift fissure
highlights.note: The fissure is a crack in the plate boundary between the North American and Eurasian plates, dived as four connected sections: Big Crack, Hall, Cathedral and Lagoon. The 'diving between two continents' framing is what sells the site and it is loosely true, but you are not touching two plates at once; the rift zone is kilometres wide and the fissure sits inside it.

highlights.label: Glacial meltwater visibility
highlights.note: Mild surprise relative to the headline: people book for the tectonic story and come back talking about the water. Meltwater filtered through lava for decades before surfacing, producing horizontal visibility reported at over 100 metres, plus bright green filamentous algae ('troll hair') in the shallow lagoon. No marine life to speak of, which is the point.

species.name: Arctic char
species.note: Rarely seen. Reported to enter the fissure around the Aug-Sep spawning period. Single operator source; unverified.

species.name: Dwarf Arctic char
species.note: A 2-10cm dwarf morph is described as resident in the Þingvallavatn system. Present year-round but very rarely noticed by divers, hence 'off' throughout rather than 'peak'. Single operator source; unverified.

trip_formats.note: Half to full day from Reykjavík, typically two dives of 30-40 minutes with a surface interval. Guide ratio is capped at 3 divers.

Format mismatch warning, and the most important field in this record. The overwhelming majority of Silfra visitors snorkel, not dive. Because max depth is 18m and typical dives run 7-12m, and because the entire point is horizontal visibility, snorkelling delivers most of the experience at a fraction of the cost and with no certification. If you are not already a drysuit diver, the scuba product is not worth the barrier. Guide ratio is capped at 6 snorkellers.

required_certs.note: Hard gate. Thingvellir National Park requires a drysuit certification, or documented proof of 10 drysuit dives within the past two years verified by an instructor. Operators will not issue without it. Wetsuits are prohibited for divers.

conditions.experience_note: The certification field understates the real barrier. Þingvellir National Park requires an autonomous-diver-equivalent certification PLUS a drysuit certification, or documented proof of 10 drysuit dives within the past two years verified by an instructor. Drysuit is mandatory and wetsuits are prohibited for divers. Hood, gloves and neoprene boots required. Max depth 18m, buddy diving mandatory, solo entry prohibited, no overhead or cave penetration, minimum age 17. Medical screening required.

operating_note: Open year-round; the water is 2-4C in every month so there is no thermal season. Winter access depends on the road to Thingvellir and on daylight, not on the site.

name: La Paz
summary: Base on the Gulf of California with a 400-animal sea lion rookery, offshore seamounts, accessible wrecks, and a separate seasonal whale shark aggregation inside the bay that is a snorkel activity rather than a dive.

highlights.label: Los Islotes sea lion rookery
highlights.note: Around 400 California sea lions and pups on a rocky islet, and the interaction is initiated by the animals. Closed 1 June to 31 August for breeding, which catches people who book Baja in summer.

highlights.label: Mobula ray aggregations
highlights.note: Under-marketed relative to the sea lions and the whale sharks. Present year-round with a Jan-May concentration, and the large schooling and breaching behaviour in the Gulf is one of the more spectacular things in the region.

highlights.label: Fang Ming, Salvatierra and C-59
highlights.note: Three intentionally sunk wrecks close to town. The Salvatierra is shallow and suits novices, which makes La Paz unusually good for a first wreck.

highlights.label: El Bajo seamount
highlights.note: Historically a famous scalloped hammerhead schooling site; the aggregation collapsed under fishing pressure in the 1980s and 90s and is reported to be recovering, best Jan-May. Ranked fourth rather than first deliberately: the marketing still leans on a reputation the site no longer fully earns.

species.name: California sea lion
species.note: Resident colony of roughly 400 including pups. Biologically present all year; the Jun-Aug gap is a site closure for breeding, carried in operating_months and in the highlight seasonality rather than faked into this array.

species.name: Whale shark
species.note: Arrives around mid-November into the shallow bay. Aggregations here are juveniles feeding at the surface. Snorkel only in practice, see trip_formats.

species.name: Mobula ray
species.note: Year-round with a Jan-May peak.

species.name: Scalloped hammerhead
species.note: El Bajo. The historic schooling aggregation was heavily reduced by fishing in the 1980s-90s and sightings are reported as increasing again. Encoded 'shoulder' not 'peak' in the best months, because the reputation runs ahead of the current reality.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Resident animals reported at La Reina.

trip_formats.note: Resort and shop-based day trips by panga or speedboat. No liveaboards are based in La Paz itself, though Sea of Cortez itineraries call here.

Format mismatch warning, and the important one for this record. The whale shark season inside La Paz bay is a regulated SNORKEL activity, not a dive. Divers book flights around 'whale sharks in La Paz' and arrive to find they will be in a wetsuit and a mask on the surface. It is a good experience; it is not scuba.
Los Islotes also runs a very large snorkel-tour market alongside the diving, on the same rock, at the same time.

conditions.experience_note: Two tiers. Inshore sites and the Salvatierra wreck are calm, shallow and suit beginners. El Bajo is an offshore seamount eight miles out with current and no reference, and operators gate it on experience. The season people do not plan for is Dec-May: water drops to 24C and as low as 18C with stronger current, which is the same window as the hammerheads and the mobulas. A 3mm is not enough in that period.

operating_note: Diving runs year-round, but Los Islotes, the single biggest draw, is closed 1 June to 31 August for sea lion breeding. That is a hard site closure inside an otherwise open destination, which is why Jun-Aug reads 'limited' rather than 'open' or 'closed'. Hurricane season overlaps the same window.

name: Palau
summary: Micronesian archipelago where incoming tides drive water across reef corners and through channels, concentrating sharks and schooling fish, alongside more than fifteen WWII wrecks and a marine lake full of stingless jellyfish.

highlights.label: Blue Corner and the channel dives
highlights.note: The product, not the hazard. Blue Corner is a coral plateau where the incoming tide stacks grey reef sharks, jack schools and Napoleon wrasse against the edge; you hook in and watch. Ulong Channel and Peleliu Express work the same way. Reef hooks are standard equipment here in a way they are almost nowhere else.

highlights.label: WWII wrecks
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: Palau is booked almost entirely on Blue Corner, and it holds over fifteen wrecks from the 1944 campaign, including the Amatsu Maru tanker, the Helmet Wreck, and a Jake seaplane sitting upright at 15m. Chuuk gets the wreck reputation; Palau quietly has both.

highlights.label: German Channel manta cleaning stations
highlights.note: Nov-Apr. Cleaning stations on sand at the channel mouth, plus Devilfish City.

highlights.label: Jellyfish Lake and Chandelier Caves
highlights.note: SNORKEL ONLY at Jellyfish Lake. A landlocked marine lake holding golden jellyfish that evolved in isolation and have lost most of their sting. The lake closed to visitors after the population collapsed during the 2015-16 drought and El Nino, and has since reopened under controlled access; confirm current status before booking around it. Chandelier Caves is a separate cavern system with air-filled chambers.

species.name: Grey reef shark
species.note: Resident year-round on the corners and in the channels. Unbaited; they hold in current for the same reason the fish do. Palau declared the world's first national shark sanctuary in 2009, which is part of why the densities persist.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Nov-Apr at German Channel and Devilfish City.

species.name: Napoleon wrasse
species.note: Large habituated individuals at Blue Corner. Endangered and heavily fished across most of its range.

species.name: Golden jellyfish
species.note: Endemic subspecies in Ongeim'l Tketau (Jellyfish Lake), snorkel only. The population crashed to near-zero during the 2015-16 El Nino drought and subsequently recovered; encoded 'shoulder' throughout rather than 'peak' because numbers have proven volatile and current status was not verified. Do not build a trip around it without checking.

trip_formats.note: Koror-based operators running fast boats to the Rock Islands. Covers Blue Corner, German Channel and the wrecks comfortably. State and dive permits are charged separately and are not trivial.
Better access to Peleliu in the south, which is exposed and often unreachable on a day boat.
Jellyfish Lake is snorkel-only by regulation; scuba is prohibited in the lake because bubbles disturb the stratified anoxic layer. Rock Islands kayak and snorkel tours are a large separate market.

required_certs.note: Standard on liveaboards; repetitive 30m+ corner dives.

conditions.experience_note: Warm and clear, but this is hook-in current diving and the corner dives are timed to the incoming tide. Peleliu Express in particular can produce serious downcurrent and is not a beginner site regardless of what a shop will sell you. Reef hook technique, negative entries and SMB deployment are all assumed. Some sheltered sites and the shallower wrecks suit Open Water divers; the sites people come for do not.

operating_note: Diveable all year with no closure. Jun-Sep is the wet season with rougher seas, visibility down to 15-20m, and exposed sites like Peleliu frequently cancelled, hence 'limited'. Dec-Apr is dry season with 40m+ visibility and is also the manta window.

name: Fakarava
summary: UNESCO Biosphere Reserve atoll 400km from Tahiti with two tidal passes, the southern one holding a permanent aggregation of several hundred grey reef sharks in a 200m-wide channel.

highlights.label: The Wall of Sharks, Tumakohua (south) pass
highlights.note: Several hundred grey reef sharks holding station in current in a 200m channel, permanently, not seasonally. Lemon sharks, hammerheads and oceanic whitetips also recorded here. There is no equivalent density of resident reef sharks in an accessible pass anywhere else.

highlights.label: Pass drift diving
highlights.note: Genuinely the product rather than a hazard. Both passes are dived on the incoming tide, dropping outside and being flushed into the lagoon. Garuae in the north is 1,600m wide, the widest channel in French Polynesia, and needs slack or incoming water. Tumakohua in the south is narrower and gentler.

highlights.label: Marbled grouper spawning aggregation
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline, and one of the great underwater events almost nobody plans for. Around the June-July full moon on an outgoing tide, marbled grouper mass in the south pass to spawn, and the resident sharks arrive to hunt them. Sometimes hundreds of sharks. Tightly date-bound: the 2026 event is reported around 29 July, so the trip has to be booked to the moon, not the month.

highlights.label: Biosphere reserve reef
highlights.note: UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1977, covering seven islands. Low population, minimal fishing pressure, and reef condition that reflects both.

species.name: Grey reef shark
species.note: Several hundred animals resident in the south pass, every month. Unbaited: they hold in the channel because the current delivers food, not because anyone feeds them. This is the strongest 'any month works' claim in the dataset.

species.name: Marbled grouper
species.note: Resident, but the spawning aggregation is the event and it is keyed to the full moon in June-July rather than to a month. Check the lunar calendar before booking.

species.name: Scalloped hammerhead
species.note: Jan-Mar reported as the peak window, at depth in the passes.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Reported year-round at sites near the north pass rather than in the shark channel itself.

species.name: Humpback whale
species.note: Aug-Oct in French Polynesian waters. In-water interaction is regulated across French Polynesia and is a surface activity where permitted; not a dive.

trip_formats.note: Rustic pensions rather than resorts, concentrated at Rotoava in the north. Format trap: Rotoava is at the NORTH pass and the Wall of Sharks is at the SOUTH pass, roughly two hours away by boat. Staying in Rotoava and expecting daily south-pass diving does not work; there are a handful of small pensions at the south end, and they book out.
Tuamotu itineraries covering Fakarava, Rangiroa and often Toau. The only format that dives both passes properly without a repositioning problem.

required_certs.note: Repetitive pass profiles at 25-30m.

conditions.experience_note: Warm and clear, but tidal current in a pass is not the same skill as reef drift. Dives are timed to the incoming tide and getting the timing wrong flushes you out of the atoll rather than into it. Depth range 5-30m. Sources put it at intermediate to advanced; Advanced is the practical floor for the south pass. Remote: Fakarava is a 70-minute flight from Tahiti and medical evacuation is a long chain.

operating_note: Open year-round; the sharks do not have a season. Nov-Apr is the wetter, warmer, more humid half with more rain and occasional cyclone risk, and May-Oct is drier. Neither closes anything.

name: Rangiroa
summary: The largest atoll in French Polynesia, dived almost entirely in two tidal passes where incoming water carries divers into the lagoon past resident sharks and a habituated bottlenose dolphin pod.

highlights.label: Tiputa Pass drift
highlights.note: The product. You drop outside on the incoming tide and get flushed through the pass into the lagoon, past everything holding in the channel. Avatoru Pass is the quieter second option. Both are timed to the tide, not the clock.

highlights.label: Resident bottlenose dolphins
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline. Rangiroa is filed under shark diving, and it holds one of the few genuinely habituated wild bottlenose pods that interact with divers in the pass rather than fleeing. They also surf the standing wave at Tiputa in the late afternoon, which is worth watching from land.

highlights.label: Multi-species shark density
highlights.note: Grey reef, silky, lemon, whitetip and blacktip in the same pass, with counts of 200+ animals reported on a single dive. Unbaited.

highlights.label: Great hammerheads
highlights.note: Dec-Mar. Great hammerheads are rare and shy almost everywhere; Rangiroa in the southern summer is one of a very small number of places to see them without bait.

species.name: Bottlenose dolphin
species.note: Resident pod at Tiputa Pass, habituated to divers over decades and known to initiate contact. Present year-round.

species.name: Grey reef shark
species.note: Holding in the pass in numbers on every tide.

species.name: Great hammerhead
species.note: Dec-Mar. Single source for the window.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Jul-Sep. Note this is the inverse of the hammerhead window, so the two headline seasonal animals cannot be combined in one trip.

species.name: Silky shark
species.note: In the blue outside the pass.

trip_formats.note: Small operators and pensions near the two passes at Avatoru and Tiputa. Diving is tide-dependent, so the daily schedule shifts through the week and there are only so many usable slots per day.
Tuamotu itineraries usually pairing Rangiroa with Fakarava.

conditions.experience_note: Warm and clear, but the passes carry serious tidal current and getting the timing wrong means being flushed out to sea rather than into the lagoon.
