Operators expect divers comfortable with drift, negative entries and blue-water ascents. Lagoon sites are a gentle alternative for less experienced divers, but they are not why anyone comes.

operating_note: Open year-round with no closure. Jun-Sep is the peak tourist season and the drier half; Dec-Mar is warmer, wetter and carries the hammerhead window. The two headline seasons pull in opposite directions, which is the useful thing to know before booking.

name: Moorea
summary: High volcanic island 17km from Tahiti with easy shallow reef diving, long-established shark-feeding sites, and a humpback whale season that is a regulated surface activity rather than a dive.

highlights.label: Lemon and blacktip shark sites
highlights.note: BAITED. Moorea has one of the longest-running shark-feeding tourism operations anywhere, at sites including Tiki Point and the area known as Lemon Shark Valley, and it has been studied as such: peer-reviewed work exists on its effect on surrounding fish populations and on bite-risk management for divers. The encounters are close and reliable precisely because they are provisioned. Whether that is acceptable is the diver's call; the dataset states it.

highlights.label: Humpback whale season
highlights.note: SNORKEL ONLY in practice. Aug-Oct, occasionally into early November. In-water whale interaction across French Polynesia is regulated and conducted from the surface with a licensed guide; scuba is not how this happens. Divers book Moorea in September expecting to dive with whales and end up on a boat with a snorkel, which is a good day out but not what they paid for.

highlights.label: Shallow lagoon and outer reef
highlights.note: Opunohu Canyons, The Rose Garden, The Aquarium. Easy, warm, shallow, and genuinely beginner-friendly, which is under-stated because Moorea gets sold on sharks. This is one of the more relaxed destinations in the dataset.

highlights.label: Rays Corridor
highlights.note: Drift dive with schooling eagle rays.

species.name: Lemon shark
species.note: Resident and reliable year-round, with the reliability coming from feeding. Sicklefin lemon shark, the Indo-Pacific species, not the Atlantic N. brevirostris seen at Tiger Beach.

species.name: Blacktip reef shark
species.note: Ubiquitous in the lagoon; the concentrated encounters are at feeding sites.

species.name: Humpback whale
species.note: Aug-Oct with the season sometimes running to 1 November. Mothers and calves in the sheltered water off the island. Surface interaction only, licensed operators, regulated approach distances.

species.name: Grey reef shark
species.note: On the outer reef, away from the feeding sites.

species.name: Spotted eagle ray
species.note: Schooling on the Rays Corridor drift.

trip_formats.note: Resort and shop-based day diving, short boat rides, two-tank mornings. Moorea is a 30-minute ferry from Tahiti so it combines easily with a wider French Polynesia trip.

Format mismatch warning. Two large snorkel markets run alongside the diving: the lagoon stingray-and-blacktip feeding excursions, which are provisioned shallow-water encounters aimed at cruise and resort guests, and the seasonal humpback whale swims. Neither is scuba, and both dominate search results for 'Moorea sharks' and 'Moorea whales'.

conditions.experience_note: Among the easiest diving in this dataset: warm, shallow, average depth around 18m, minimal current, short boat rides. The Rose Garden is the one site sources single out as needing experience. The real briefing that matters is behavioural, not technical: these are provisioned sharks at close range and the operator's positioning rules exist for a reason. Peer-reviewed work on bite-risk management in French Polynesian shark-feeding tourism exists precisely because the risk profile differs from unbaited diving.

operating_note: Open year-round with no closure. Nov-Apr is the warmer, wetter half with occasional cyclone risk; May-Oct is drier and also covers the whale season.

name: South Ari Atoll
summary: Central Maldivian atoll holding one of the few year-round resident whale shark aggregations in the world, inside a marine protected area, alongside standard Maldivian thila, channel and wreck diving.

highlights.label: Resident whale sharks
highlights.note: The distinguishing claim, and it is the opposite of the usual whale shark story. Along Maamigili reef inside the South Ari MPA the animals are present year-round with near-daily sightings, not seasonal. Contrast Hanifaru in Baa Atoll, where whale sharks are a monsoon-window event and scuba is banned outright: here you can dive with them, in any month.

highlights.label: Reef mantas at Madivaru
highlights.note: Dec-May, on the south side of Rangali Kandu. Monsoon-driven: cleaning stations activate on whichever side of the atoll is downcurrent of the prevailing wind, so the productive side flips through the year.

highlights.label: Machchafushi wreck
highlights.note: Sunk 1998, intact and heavily colonised. Under-mentioned relative to the megafauna.

highlights.label: Thilas and channel drifts
highlights.note: Submerged pinnacles inside the atoll with soft coral and schooling fish. What most of the tank time actually is.

species.name: Whale shark
species.note: Resident, near-daily sightings all year, with larger congregations Dec-Mar during the northeast monsoon. The animals shift west Dec-Apr and east May-Nov with the monsoon, so the productive stretch of reef moves rather than emptying. Unusually for a whale shark site, these are not provisioned.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Dec-May at Madivaru (Manta Point). Monsoon-driven cleaning station activity.

species.name: Grey reef shark
species.note: On the channel dives.

trip_formats.note: Resort or local-island guesthouse on Dhigurah or Maamigili. Guesthouses on the local islands are dramatically cheaper than the resorts and sit closer to the whale shark reef.
Central-atoll Maldives itineraries. More sites, less time on the specific stretch of reef where the whale sharks are.

Large snorkel-excursion market on the same Maamigili reef, often heavily crowded with boats when an animal is spotted. Unlike Hanifaru, scuba is permitted here, so the snorkel product is a choice rather than the only option.

conditions.experience_note: Warm, 5-30m, and much of it is genuinely beginner-friendly. Channel dives are drift dives with real current and are the step up. The whale shark encounters happen shallow along the reef edge, often with heavy boat traffic overhead, so surface awareness matters more than depth skill. Do not touch or block the animals; the MPA has a code of conduct.

operating_note: Open year-round. Jun-Sep is the southwest monsoon with more rain, wind and reduced visibility, and the western sites blow out, so those read 'limited'. The whale sharks are there regardless; the diving around them is just less pleasant.

name: Baa Atoll
summary: UNESCO Biosphere Reserve atoll in the western Maldives containing Hanifaru Bay, a funnel-shaped plankton trap where reef mantas and whale sharks mass-feed during the southwest monsoon, under a snorkel-only regime.

highlights.label: Hanifaru Bay manta aggregation
highlights.note: SNORKEL ONLY. Scuba diving is banned in the bay. The bay's keyhole shape funnels plankton into a dead end on the right tide, concentrating it densely enough to trigger mass feeding, including cyclone feeding where dozens of mantas chain-loop through the same column. Access is by ranger-controlled token: 45 minutes in the water, maximum 45 people on site, maximum 5 vessels, one guide per 10 snorkellers.

highlights.label: Whale sharks at Hanifaru
highlights.note: Same aggregation, same snorkel-only rule, same tokens. Present alongside the mantas when the plankton density is high enough. Less reliable than the mantas and not the reason to book.

highlights.label: Thila and channel diving elsewhere in the atoll
highlights.note: The part that answers 'so what do I actually dive'. Baa Atoll's submerged pinnacles (thilas) and channels carry manta cleaning stations, reef sharks and soft coral, and these ARE divable on scuba. If you book Baa for the mantas, this is where your tank time goes.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Present in the Maldives year-round; the Hanifaru mass-feeding aggregation runs May-December with the strongest conditions late July to early October, particularly around full and new moon. Aggregation is driven by lunar tidal cycles concentrating plankton, so the moon matters more than the month.

species.name: Whale shark
species.note: At Hanifaru during the aggregation. Note the contrast with South Ari Atoll, where whale sharks are resident year-round and divable on scuba.

species.name: Grey reef shark
species.note: On the atoll channels, not in Hanifaru.

trip_formats.note: The only legal way to be in Hanifaru Bay. 45 minutes in the water per token, $20-30, ranger-supervised, 45 people maximum on site, 5 vessels maximum, one guide per 10 snorkellers. This is the single most important field in the record: a certified diver cannot dive Hanifaru at any price.
Resort-based diving on the atoll's thilas and channels, with Hanifaru added as a snorkel excursion when conditions and tokens allow.

Maldives itineraries include Baa in season, but liveaboards cannot anchor at Hanifaru: they stop at Dharavandhoo and guests transfer by taxi boat. Confirm that a boat actually holds Hanifaru tokens before booking on that basis.

conditions.experience_note: Hanifaru itself demands nothing beyond being able to snorkel: max depth around 20m and the animals feed at the surface. Visibility during the aggregation is poor by Maldivian standards precisely because the water is thick with plankton, which surprises people expecting blue water. Atoll channel diving is current-driven and a step up. Do not touch or chase the mantas; the rangers enforce it.

operating_note: The atoll is open and divable all year, but Hanifaru Bay itself is a seasonal southwest-monsoon phenomenon running roughly May to December. Outside that window the resorts and dive sites operate normally and the bay is simply empty, so Jan-Apr reads 'limited' rather than 'closed': you can go, you will dive, you will not see the thing Baa Atoll is famous for.

name: Red Sea North
summary: Sheltered northern end of the Egyptian Red Sea holding the best-known wreck in recreational diving, plus hard coral walls and drop-offs, dived year-round from resorts and short liveaboards.

highlights.label: SS Thistlegorm
highlights.note: British armed merchant ship bombed in 1941 with her cargo holds still full of Bedford trucks, BSA motorcycles, rifles and rolling stock. Rediscovered by Cousteau. The reason most people book the northern Red Sea, and it earns it: cargo wrecks this intact and this accessible do not really exist elsewhere.

highlights.label: Abu Nuhas wreck cluster
highlights.note: Four wrecks on one reef, including the Giannis D and the Carnatic. Under-mentioned next to the Thistlegorm but delivers more wreck diving per boat day.

highlights.label: Hard coral walls at Ras Mohammed
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline. The north is booked on wrecks, and Shark and Yolanda Reef at Ras Mohammed is one of the densest fish-and-hard-coral walls anywhere in the region, with summer schooling aggregations of barracuda, snapper and batfish.

species.name: Bluespotted ribbontail ray
species.note: Ubiquitous on sand patches. Included as one of the genuinely reliable northern Red Sea animals rather than a headline.

species.name: Napoleon wrasse
species.note: Habituated individuals at several northern sites.

species.name: Whitetip reef shark
species.note: The northern Red Sea is not shark diving. Encoded as unreliable in all months deliberately: the shark itineraries are in the south, and conflating the two is the most common Red Sea booking error.

trip_formats.note: Very large resort market at Sharm el-Sheikh, Dahab and Hurghada. Day boats reach Ras Mohammed and the Straits of Tiran; the Thistlegorm is a long day or an overnight from Sharm.
Short northern itineraries covering Thistlegorm, Abu Nuhas, Ras Mohammed and the Straits of Tiran. The efficient way to dive the wrecks properly rather than as a single rushed visit.

Dahab in particular is a shore-diving town, including the Blue Hole. Note that the Blue Hole's arch is a technical dive at 55m with a significant fatality history and is not the same activity as the shallow shore dive of the same name.

required_certs.note: The Thistlegorm's holds are routinely entered on guided dives, but the cargo decks are an overhead environment with silt and entanglement hazards.
Thistlegorm sits at 16-30m and is usually dived twice in a day.

conditions.experience_note: The most beginner-accessible destination in this dataset alongside Cozumel and Moalboal, and that accessibility is a condition rather than a highlight: warm, clear, minimal current at most sites, extensive shore diving, and one of the cheapest places in the world to certify. Two real gates. The Thistlegorm can carry strong current and its cargo holds are a genuine overhead environment. And winter water drops to 21-23C, which calls for 5mm or 7mm and surprises people expecting Egypt to be warm in January.

operating_note: Open year-round with no closure; this is the sheltered end of the Red Sea and the reason the north has a twelve-month resort economy while the southern offshore itineraries do not. Winter brings wind and cooler water, summer brings heat and crowds, neither stops the diving.

name: Brothers, Daedalus and Elphinstone
summary: Three isolated offshore reefs rising from deep water in the southern Egyptian Red Sea, reachable only by liveaboard, dived for oceanic sharks on sheer walls and for two wrecks stacked on one island's reef slope.

highlights.label: Oceanic whitetip sharks
highlights.note: The animal that makes this itinerary distinct rather than just another Red Sea trip. Oceanic whitetips are a genuinely open-ocean species and Elphinstone and Daedalus are among very few places they can be dived reliably, typically hanging in the blue near the safety stop. Strongest Jun-Nov.

highlights.label: Offshore pinnacle walls
highlights.note: All three sites are isolated reefs surrounded by deep water, dived as drifts along vertical walls dense with soft coral and gorgonians. The topography, not the sharks, is what most divers describe afterwards.

highlights.label: Numidia and Aida, Big Brother
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: this is sold as a shark itinerary and Big Brother carries two wrecks on the same reef slope. The Numidia in particular runs steeply from about 8m to past 80m, so the same wreck is a recreational dive and a technical one depending on how far down you go.

highlights.label: Hammerheads and threshers
highlights.note: Scalloped hammerheads at Daedalus, best on early dives in the warmer months. Brothers has a reputation for thresher sharks at dawn. Both are less reliable than the oceanic whitetips.

species.name: Oceanic whitetip shark
species.note: Jun-Nov at Elphinstone and Daedalus. Critically endangered globally. Unbaited, and notably curious rather than shy, which is why encounters happen in the blue rather than on the reef.

species.name: Scalloped hammerhead
species.note: Daedalus, typically deep and on the first dive of the day.

species.name: Thresher shark
species.note: Brothers, reported at dawn. Genus-level because sources do not specify which thresher. Encoded unreliable in all months: this is a bonus, not a product, and it is nothing like the daily reliability at Malapascua.

species.name: Grey reef shark
species.note: Resident on the offshore reefs; the encoded gaps reflect when boats are there rather than the animal, and are held down deliberately because access and biology are hard to separate in the sources.

trip_formats.note: The only access; all three reefs are offshore with no land base. Around 16 dives across 7 nights, three day dives daily. Night diving is prohibited in the marine park. Government reef taxes are charged on top, roughly $90.

required_certs.note: Deep repetitive wall profiles across a week.
Sites regularly work past 30m, and the Numidia continues well beyond recreational limits.

conditions.experience_note: Operators state a minimum of 30 logged dives on top of Open Water, and that is a floor rather than a recommendation. These are isolated pinnacles in open ocean: current runs hard and unpredictably around the tips, ascents are frequently in blue water with no reference, and if you get swept off the reef there is nothing downstream. Overnight open-sea crossings mean the itinerary itself gets cancelled or rerouted in wind. Winter water at 21-23C needs 5-7mm.

operating_note: Sources disagree on whether this is a closure or just bad weather. Some operators list the itinerary as running year-round; others describe winter wind limiting access to the offshore sites, and the Egyptian marine park has historically restricted Brothers and Daedalus in the winter months. Encoded 'limited' for Dec-Feb rather than 'closed' because the evidence does not support a hard closure. See OQ-29. Note the tension in the two arrays: the best shark months (Jun-Nov) are not the best condition months (Mar-May, Sep-Nov).

name: Ningaloo Reef
region: Exmouth and Coral Bay, Western Australia
summary: 260km fringing reef running along a remote stretch of the Western Australian coast, close enough to shore to swim to, best known for a whale shark aggregation that is a licensed snorkel activity rather than a dive.

highlights.label: Whale shark aggregation
highlights.note: SNORKEL ONLY. This is the single most important field in the record. The whale shark season is a tightly licensed surface swim: spotter aircraft locate the animal, the boat holds off, and groups of up to 10 swimmers enter with a guide. Scuba is not how this works, and roughly 41,000 people did it in 2025. The aggregation follows the mass coral spawn, usually March or April, which is what draws the animals in.

highlights.label: Exmouth Navy Pier
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline, and a big one. Ningaloo is booked entirely on whale sharks, and the Navy Pier is regularly rated among the best shore dives in the world: a working military jetty whose pylons are packed with soft coral, sponges, nudibranchs, wobbegongs and a resident giant grouper at 15m. Access is controlled: a single operator holds it, dives are tide-dependent, and federal police identity verification is required in advance.

highlights.label: Year-round reef mantas
highlights.note: Also under-marketed. Mantas with wingspans reported to 8m are present in the Coral Bay lagoon in every month, unlike the whale sharks, and unlike almost every other manta destination in this dataset there is no season to plan around.

highlights.label: Humpback whale season
highlights.note: SNORKEL ONLY where in-water interaction is permitted at all. Jul-Oct, with over 40,000 animals reported passing annually. Same licensing structure as the whale sharks.

species.name: Whale shark
species.note: Tours run March to end of June from Coral Bay and to August from Exmouth, with sightings sometimes continuing into October and, in recent years, early November. Peak May-June. Unbaited: the animals come for the post-spawn plankton bloom, not for anything the operators put in the water. Most operators offer a free return if no shark is found.

species.name: Reef manta ray
species.note: Year-round in the Coral Bay lagoon. Wingspans reported to 8m.

species.name: Humpback whale
species.note: Jul-Oct, over 40,000 animals annually on the Western Australian migration.

species.name: Giant grouper
species.note: A resident individual at the Navy Pier known locally as the BFG, at around 15m.

trip_formats.note: The whale shark and humpback swims. Licensed operators only, spotter aircraft, up to 10 swimmers in the water at a time from boats of around 20 guests, regulated approach distances. Twelve or so licensed whale shark operators between Exmouth and Coral Bay. If whale sharks are the reason for the trip, a diving certification buys you nothing.

Navy Pier is a shore dive but is not casually accessible: one operator holds it, dives are timed to slack tide, and identity verification through federal police is required in advance because it is an operational military facility. Book weeks ahead.
Boat diving to the Muiron Islands and Lighthouse Bay out of Exmouth, plus lagoon and outer-reef sites from Coral Bay.

The lagoon fringing reef sits 2-4m deep metres from the beach, with coral bommies swimmable directly from shore at Oyster Stacks, Tantabiddi and Osprey Sanctuary. One of the few world-class reefs you can reach without a boat or a tank.

conditions.experience_note: Undemanding for the most part: shallow lagoon, mild current, warm water, and sources state all certification levels are catered for including snorkellers and freedivers. Two specific caveats. Navy Pier visibility is genuinely poor at 3-10m and the dive is tide-locked, so it is a silt-and-timing dive rather than a blue-water one. And the whale shark swim demands swimming fitness rather than dive skill: you enter ahead of a moving animal and keep pace at the surface, repeatedly, over several hours. A 3mm suit is the standard recommendation.

operating_note: Diving and snorkelling continue year-round, but the whale shark tour fleet only operates March to June or August depending on the base, and the humpback swims July to October. Nov-Feb is the Australian summer wet and cyclone season on this coast with the megafauna gone, so those months read 'limited': the reef is still there, the industry is largely not.

name: Ribbon Reefs (Northern Great Barrier Reef)
summary: Chain of narrow reefs running along the outer edge of the northern Great Barrier Reef between Cairns and Lizard Island, dived from liveaboards, with a June-July dwarf minke whale season found nowhere else.

highlights.label: Dwarf minke whale season
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline, and a strong one. The Great Barrier Reef is a byword for coral, and the Ribbon Reefs hold the only predictable, permitted in-water dwarf minke whale interaction in the world, for two months a year. The whales approach the boats voluntarily; swimmers hold a surface rope and the animal decides how close to come.

highlights.label: Outer-edge ribbon reef system
highlights.note: The outer ribbons take clear oceanic water off the continental shelf and are in materially better condition than the inshore day-trip reefs out of Cairns and Port Douglas, which is the distinction almost no booking page draws.

highlights.label: Cod Hole potato cod
highlights.note: Ribbon Reef No. 10. Very large habituated potato cod that approach divers directly. Historically a fed site; feeding is now restricted under Marine Park rules, so treat any 'cod feed' description with caution.

species.name: Dwarf minke whale
species.note: June and July only. An undescribed subspecies of common minke whale. Interaction is governed by a Code of Practice: swimmers hold surface ropes, must stay 30m from a whale and may not swim toward one; the whale closes the distance or does not. Only a small number of GBRMPA-endorsed operators hold the permit, and trips feed the Minke Whale Project's research.

species.name: Potato cod
species.note: Resident habituated individuals at the Cod Hole. Habituation originates in historical feeding, though the encounter today is not baited.

trip_formats.note: The standard format and effectively the only way to reach the outer ribbons. 11-26 dives depending on length. Several itineraries fly one leg to or from Lizard Island rather than steaming both ways.

Format note for the minke season specifically. Both snorkelling and scuba are permitted, and non-divers can join, but the interaction protocol is a surface rope line, so in practice the whale encounter is a snorkel activity that divers also happen to be certified for. Divers need Open Water plus 10 ocean dives, 5 in the last 12 months. If minkes are the goal, certification is not the gate.

Format mismatch warning. The enormous Cairns and Port Douglas day-boat market goes to inshore and mid-shelf reefs, NOT the Ribbon Reefs, and not to minke whales. 'Great Barrier Reef day trip' and 'Ribbon Reefs' are different products at very different quality levels, and the search results do not distinguish them.

required_certs.note: Long liveaboard days with up to 26 dives.

conditions.experience_note: Straightforward reef diving by the standards of this dataset: moderate current, warm water, good visibility. The recency requirement matters more than the card level, with operators asking for 5 dives in the last 12 months. Winter (the minke window) is the coolest water at around 23C. Stinger season roughly November to May brings box jellyfish and Irukandji inshore; full-body suits are standard and this is a real consideration on the shallower sites.

operating_note: Liveaboards run year-round. Dec-Feb is the wet season and cyclone window in Far North Queensland, when trips get cancelled and sea state deteriorates, hence 'limited'. The minke whale season is a hard two months, June and July, and those trips sell out a year ahead because only a small number of endorsed operators hold the permit.

name: Coral Sea (Osprey Reef)
summary: Isolated oceanic atoll rising from 1,000m of water 350km northeast of Cairns, in a separate marine park from the Great Barrier Reef, dived for wall topography, extreme visibility and a baited shark feed.

highlights.label: Thousand-metre walls
highlights.note: Osprey is a seamount, not part of the continental shelf reef. Walls drop roughly 1,000m into blue water with visibility reported up to 100m, which is a different visual experience entirely from the Great Barrier Reef 350km to the southwest. Swim-throughs, caves, ledges and bommies along the rim.

highlights.label: North Horn shark feed
highlights.note: BAITED. A bin of bait is lowered into a natural amphitheatre at North Horn while divers sit on the ledge; up to 50 reef sharks converge. Run when conditions permit rather than on schedule. This is the single most-photographed thing in the Coral Sea and its baited nature is usually a footnote.

highlights.label: Large resident groupers
highlights.note: Giant potato cod and Queensland groper, plus bumphead parrotfish, coral trout and trevally on the rim. Under-mentioned next to the sharks.

species.name: Grey reef shark
species.note: Resident on the reef and encountered naturally on the walls, but the dense aggregation people book for is the North Horn feed. Encoded 'baited' because that is what the headline encounter is; the animals are here regardless.

species.name: Silvertip shark
species.note: Also at the feed.

species.name: Whitetip reef shark
species.note: Encountered on the walls independent of the feed.

species.name: Scalloped hammerhead
species.note: Described as occasional with no season given. Encoded unreliable in all months rather than inventing a window.

trip_formats.note: The only access, and it is a genuine expedition leg: roughly 20 hours of open-ocean crossing from the Ribbon Reefs, done overnight. Usually sold as a Coral Sea extension to a Great Barrier Reef itinerary, 15 dives on a 4-day trip up to 26 on a 7-day. Many itineraries fly one leg via Lizard Island.

required_certs.note: Deep wall profiles, up to 26 dives per trip.

conditions.experience_note: Advanced is stated as a requirement rather than a preference. The specific demands are wall diving with no bottom reference over 1,000m of water, live-boat drops and tender pickups, and long open-ocean crossings to reach a reef with no land, no shelter and no medical facility within a day. The visibility that makes it spectacular also makes depth easy to misjudge.

operating_note: Trips run year-round but the crossing is the constraint: 20 hours of open ocean each way means the Coral Sea leg is dropped or rerouted in weather far more often than the sheltered Ribbon Reefs are. Dec-Feb is cyclone season in the region, hence 'limited'.

name: Yonaguni
summary: Japan's westernmost island, 111km from Taiwan, sitting in the Kuroshio current, with a winter hammerhead aggregation and a large stepped rock formation whose origin is disputed.

highlights.label: Winter hammerhead aggregation
highlights.note: Ranked first on its own merits, not as a consolation to the monument. Scalloped hammerheads school off Irizaki January to March. The trade is brutal and explicit: the schooling season is also the coldest water of the year (around 23C) and the strongest Kuroshio current. There is no comfortable way to dive this.

highlights.label: Yonaguni Monument (Kaitei Iseki)
highlights.note: CONTESTED ORIGIN, and the dataset does not take a side. A stepped rock mass roughly 290m by 120m and 26m high, top terrace at about 5m and base at about 25m, 100m off Arakawabana Cape. Masaaki Kimura (Ryukyus) argues for human construction, citing near-vertical walls, apparent drainage channels, retaining walls and carved features. Geologists argue the local sandstone fractures along bedding planes and joints to produce exactly these forms naturally; one cited position is that it is 95% natural with possible human modification. Encoded as `formation` because the geological structure is the draw regardless of who or what made it.

highlights.label: Kuroshio current diving
highlights.note: The current is the reason both of the above exist: it delivers the hammerheads and it carved or exposed the monument. It is also why the island is a difficult destination rather than a popular one.

species.name: Scalloped hammerhead
species.note: Jan-Mar schooling off Irizaki. Single source for the window; no research literature located. Unbaited.

species.name: Hammerhead shark (unresolved species)
species.note: Sources refer only to 'hammerheads' without consistently resolving species. Retained as a separate genus-level entry rather than assuming every reported animal is S. lewini. Merge these two entries once a source confirms.

trip_formats.note: Small local operators; boats leave Irizaki harbour, nicknamed Shark Dock, and reach the monument in about 20 minutes. Getting to Yonaguni is the hard part: flights via Naha or Ishigaki, and the island is 2,000km from Tokyo. Very few English-speaking operators.

conditions.experience_note: One of the two or three most demanding destinations in this dataset. The Kuroshio runs hard and sources recommend Advanced plus roughly 100 logged dives. The hammerhead season is winter: coldest water, strongest current, roughest surface conditions, and dives are frequently cancelled. The monument itself is shallow (5-25m) but sits in the same water. Remote island, limited medical support.

operating_note: No formal closure, but two separate limiting periods. Jan-Mar is the hammerhead window and also winter: north-east monsoon wind cancels a high proportion of days, so you can book a week and dive twice. Jul-Sep is typhoon season in the Ryukyus. This is the sharpest example in the dataset of the thing you came for and the conditions that let you see it being in direct opposition.

name: Tiger Beach
summary: Shallow sandbank off the west end of Grand Bahama where sharks are baited to divers kneeling on white sand in around 6 metres of water, producing the most reliable large-shark encounters anywhere.

highlights.label: Baited tiger shark encounter
highlights.note: BAITED. Divers kneel on the sandbank in a V formation facing into the current with a professional feeder at the point, and tigers are fed to bring them in. Typically four or five animals in the water, up to fifteen at the best of it. This is the fact that determines whether the destination is for you, and it is usually buried in the small print.

highlights.label: Lemon and Caribbean reef shark density
highlights.note: Under-advertised relative to the tigers, and what most of the dive actually consists of. Twenty to thirty lemon sharks and dozens of Caribbean reef sharks on a typical dive, at close range in 6m of clear water. Several divers report this as the more interesting part.

highlights.label: Great hammerheads
highlights.note: Dec-Mar. Also baited. Great hammerheads are shy and rarely seen elsewhere at close range, which makes this window the reason a lot of photographers book the trip rather than the tigers.

species.name: Tiger shark
species.note: Resident population, present all year, with more animals reported Oct-Jan. Typically 4-5 in the water, up to 15. Encounters depend on bait; this is not an animal that would otherwise approach a group of kneeling divers.

species.name: Lemon shark
species.note: 20-30 on a typical dive, around 3m long.

species.name: Caribbean reef shark
species.note: Present in dozens on most dives.

species.name: Great hammerhead
species.note: Dec-Mar. Critically endangered globally; the Bahamas has a national shark sanctuary, which is part of why the aggregation persists here.

species.name: Nurse shark
species.note: Occasional.

trip_formats.note: The dominant format. Departs Freeport, Grand Bahama. Multiple long shallow dives per day on the same site, which is unusual and is what makes the encounters reliable rather than lucky.
Some land-based operators run day trips from West End, Grand Bahama. Fewer hours in the water on a site where time is the whole variable.

Snorkelling is offered and the site is shallow enough to make it viable, but the encounter is designed around a seated formation on the bottom. Surface snorkelling over baited large sharks is a materially different proposition and should not be treated as an equivalent product.

conditions.experience_note: Technically among the easiest diving in this dataset: around 6m on a flat white sandbank, exceptional visibility, no depth or gas pressure. Sources describe it as suitable for all levels including snorkellers. The demand is entirely psychological and procedural: you kneel still, in formation, facing into current, surrounded by large sharks, and you follow the feeder's briefing exactly. Divers who are uncomfortable staying motionless or who reach for a camera at the wrong moment are the problem, not the depth.

operating_note: Runs year-round. Jun-Sep is Atlantic hurricane season and individual trips get cancelled or rerouted, hence 'limited'. Note the two peaks pull in different directions: Oct-Jan for tiger numbers, Dec-Mar for great hammerheads, with Dec-Jan the overlap.

name: Azores
summary: Mid-Atlantic volcanic archipelago with offshore seamounts rising into blue water, dived in a short summer window for chummed blue and mako shark encounters and for predictable devil ray aggregations.

highlights.label: Blue and shortfin mako sharks
highlights.note: BAITED, using what operators describe as minimal chumming, with no cage, in open blue water off Pico. Reported sighting success above 90% in season and up to 20 blue sharks on a dive. Touching and feeding the animals is prohibited; the chum brings them, the divers do not interact. This is the clearest case in the dataset of a destination that is entirely honest about baiting and still worth encoding, because the alternative framing ('seen with surprising regularity') appears on other pages for the same dives.

highlights.label: Devil ray aggregations on the seamounts
highlights.note: Under-marketed relative to the sharks and arguably the better dive. Sicklefin and spinetail devil rays gather predictably at Princesa Alice Bank near Faial and Pico, and at Ambrósio near Santa Maria, June to October. Mature adults, which suggests the sites matter for mating or birthing.

highlights.label: Cetacean diversity
highlights.note: Up to 20 species recorded, including sperm whales resident year-round and blue whales passing March to May. SURFACE ONLY for whales: whale watching is conducted from boats, though swimming with dolphins is permitted. Not a dive.

highlights.label: Volcanic seamounts and Princesa Alice
highlights.note: Princesa Alice Bank is a submerged seamount roughly 45 nautical miles offshore, rising to about 35m from very deep water. The dive is a blue-water hang over a pinnacle with no reference in any direction.

species.name: Blue shark
species.note: July to mid-October off Pico. Up to 20 animals per dive with over 90% success. Chummed.

species.name: Shortfin mako
species.note: Same dives as the blues but far less frequent. Endangered globally.

species.name: Sicklefin devil ray
species.note: Jun-Oct at Princesa Alice and Ambrósio. Unbaited, and the aggregations are described as easy to predict, which is unusual for a pelagic ray.

species.name: Sperm whale
species.note: Resident population. Surface encounters only; this is a whale-watching activity, not a dive.

species.name: Blue whale
species.note: March-May only, on migration. Surface only.

trip_formats.note: The blue shark and Princesa Alice dives are offshore day expeditions rather than normal boat dives: long crossings, one or two dives, maximum 75 minutes per tank. Weather-dependent to a degree that inshore diving is not.
Inshore diving on volcanic reef, arches and wrecks around Faial, Pico and Santa Maria fills the days when the offshore trips cannot run. Plan for that, because they frequently cannot.
Whale watching is a large separate surface market. Swimming with dolphins is permitted; swimming with whales is not.

required_certs.note: Not required in the summer shark window at 21-25C, but Azorean water outside July-October is North Atlantic cold.

conditions.experience_note: Operators state Advanced plus at least 50 logged dives and a minimum age of 18 for the shark dives, with a mandatory check dive before you are taken offshore. The specific demand is blue-water diving: no bottom, no reference, no visual horizon, with large sharks and a chum slick, 45 nautical miles from land. This is a much higher bar than the water temperature and visibility suggest.

operating_note: The offshore diving that defines the Azores has a hard summer window: blue shark trips run July to mid-October, devil rays June to October. Outside that, inshore diving continues in spring and autumn with 10m visibility and cold water, and effectively stops in midwinter. Encoded 'closed' for Jan-Feb and December because the offshore operators do not run and there is nothing recognisable as an Azores dive trip; 'limited' in the shoulders where inshore diving is possible but the seamounts are not.

name: Aliwal Shoal
summary: Fossilised sandstone reef 5km off Umkomaas on the KwaZulu-Natal coast, reached by surf launch, with a winter ragged-tooth shark aggregation and a well-established baited shark diving industry.

highlights.label: Ragged-tooth shark aggregation
highlights.note: June to November, unbaited. Sand tiger sharks (called ragged-tooth or 'raggies' locally) gather on the reef and in the gullies, particularly at Cathedral. They look ferocious and are placid. The aggregation is the thing that made Aliwal's reputation, and it is a natural one, which is worth separating from the baited diving below.

highlights.label: Baited blacktip and tiger shark dives
highlights.note: BAITED, cage-free. A baited drum or ball is deployed and divers drift freely with it in blue water; up to 50 oceanic blacktips around a single bait ball is reported. Tiger sharks have been dived here since around 2002. Cage diving exists separately in KwaZulu-Natal for non-divers. Described by operators themselves as high-energy shark diving, and a meaningful number of divers decline it on principle.

highlights.label: Fossilised dune reef
highlights.note: Under-mentioned relative to the sharks. Aliwal is a drowned sandstone dune with caves, gullies and swim-throughs, carrying soft coral, potato bass, morays, pipefish and rays. Divers who come only for the shark dives skip it.

highlights.label: Sardine Run
highlights.note: June-July. Millions of sardines moving north along the KwaZulu-Natal coast with the predator activity that follows. Note the scope difference: the Sardine Run is a mobile coastal event covering hundreds of kilometres, usually chased from dedicated boats further south, not a dive you do at Aliwal Shoal itself.

species.name: Ragged-tooth shark
species.note: Jun-Nov, though the operator notes climate variation has been extending their presence beyond the traditional window. Unbaited: they are on the reef because they aggregate there, not because anyone put food in the water.

species.name: Oceanic blacktip shark
species.note: Year-round. Up to 50 animals around a bait ball. The species is present regardless; the density is manufactured.

species.name: Tiger shark
species.note: Nov-Mar, warm-water months. Dived here on baited drums since roughly 2002.

species.name: Bull shark
species.note: Known locally as Zambezi shark. Year-round, though the dedicated bull shark diving in this region is at Protea Banks rather than Aliwal.

species.name: Humpback whale
species.note: Passing on the KwaZulu-Natal migration through the southern winter. Surface and boat sightings; not an in-water product.

trip_formats.note: Operators in Umkomaas, roughly an hour south of Durban. Baited shark dives and reef dives are sold as separate products; do not assume one includes the other.

Sardine Run trips are a separate dedicated product in June-July, run as a chase along the coast from purpose-fitted boats, often further south. Booking Aliwal in June does not get you the Sardine Run.

conditions.experience_note: The distinctive hazard is getting there. Access is by rigid inflatable surf launch through the breakers at Umkomaas, which is genuinely rough, occasionally aborted, and unlike anything most divers have done. Once out, the shoal carries strong current and the baited dives are conducted drifting in blue water with no reference and multiple large sharks in a stimulated state, following a strict briefing. Winter water drops to around 19C. Visibility is highly variable and can collapse after rain.

operating_note: Runs year-round with no closure, but the surf launch means individual days are lost to sea state far more often than at a sheltered destination. The two headline seasons are opposed: ragged-tooth Jun-Nov in cold water, tiger sharks Nov-Mar in warm water, overlapping only in November.

name: Malta, Gozo and Comino
summary: Three Mediterranean islands with clear water, extensive shore access, a set of scuttled and wartime wrecks across the full depth range from novice to trimix, and limestone caves and tunnels.

highlights.label: Wreck diving across every depth tier
highlights.note: The genuinely distinctive thing: Malta has wrecks graded from 12m to well past 100m, so the same destination serves a newly certified diver and a trimix team. The Rozi and P29 at Cirkewwa are shallow and shore-accessible; the Um El Faroud, a 110m former Libyan oil tanker, is a deeper recreational penetration dive with cut entry and exit holes; HMS Maori, Stubborn and the deeper wartime wrecks continue past recreational limits.

highlights.label: Caves, tunnels and swim-throughs
highlights.note: Santa Marija Caves on Comino has more than ten connected caverns. The Inland Sea on Gozo is a natural lagoon joined to the open Mediterranean by an 80m rock tunnel that you swim through into deep blue water, which is one of the more theatrical entries in diving.

highlights.label: Blue Hole and the Azure Window collapse site
highlights.note: Gozo's Blue Hole is a natural limestone shaft opening onto the reef. The Azure Window arch above it collapsed into the sea in March 2017; the resulting boulder field is now itself a dive site. Marketing photographs of the intact arch are still in circulation, so this is worth knowing before you arrive expecting it.

highlights.label: Shore-accessible walls and reef
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline: Malta is booked as a wreck destination, and it is one of the best shore-diving destinations in Europe. Visibility around Gozo runs to 30m, entries are from rocky platforms rather than boats, and a diver with a car and a buddy can fill a week without booking a boat.

species.name: Dusky grouper
species.note: Endangered in the Mediterranean and heavily fished; present around the wrecks and reef.

trip_formats.note: The defining format. Most named sites including the Rozi, P29, Blue Hole, Inland Sea and Cirkewwa reef are shore entries. Hire a van, fill tanks locally, dive on your own schedule. Very few destinations of this quality work this way.
Boat diving reaches Comino's caves and the deeper offshore wrecks. Large operator market with a wide quality range and a lot of training traffic.

required_certs.note: The Um El Faroud has cut penetration holes and is routinely entered; that is an overhead environment regardless of how well lit it is.
Several of the named wrecks sit at or past 40m.
The deeper wartime wrecks are beyond air limits and are technical dives, not deep recreational ones.

conditions.experience_note: Easy conditions and hard options in the same place, which is the thing to understand. Shore entries over rock can be awkward in swell, and there is minimal current, no significant marine hazard and reliable visibility. The risk profile comes entirely from what you choose to dive: Malta has a long list of deep wreck fatalities among divers who scaled up faster than their training. Water drops to 14-15C in late winter, so year-round diving here means drysuit diving.

operating_note: Apr-Oct is the season, with the warmest water and the calmest sea. Diving continues through winter but water falls to 14-15C and the operator base thins out, hence 'limited' rather than 'closed' for Dec-Mar: the islands are dived year-round by drysuit divers and by technical teams, just not by the holiday market.

name: Oahu
summary: The most populated Hawaiian island, dived mainly for a cluster of deliberately sunk wrecks and a WWII aircraft off the south shore, with a separate commercial shark-tour industry running out of Haleiwa on the north shore.

highlights.label: South shore wreck cluster
highlights.note: The reason to dive Oahu rather than the other islands. Five accessible wrecks within a short boat ride: the YO-257 and San Pedro dived as a pair, the 50m Sea Tiger sitting upright with open hatches, the Nashua tug at 20m, and the Corsair. Nothing else in Hawai'i has this density.

highlights.label: The Corsair
highlights.note: A WWII F4U Corsair fighter that ditched intact and sits on open sand at 33m with propeller, cockpit and tail recognisable. Distinct from the scuttled ships: this is an actual loss, not an artificial reef, and garden eels and leaf scorpionfish have colonised the sand around it.

highlights.label: Frogfish and nudibranchs on the wrecks
highlights.note: Surprise relative to the headline. Oahu is booked as wreck diving and the wrecks are covered in macro subjects, including frogfish described as reaching volleyball size, plus nudibranchs, day octopus and leaf scorpionfish.

highlights.label: Haleiwa shark tours
highlights.note: SPLIT PRODUCT, and mostly not scuba. Two distinct offerings run about 3 miles off Haleiwa: cage tours, which are snorkel-based in a surface cage and explicitly use bait, and cage-free open-ocean swims, whose dominant operator states it does not chum and works from behaviour instead. Neither is a scuba dive. Sandbar and Galapagos sharks are the common species. Worth noting that some Native Hawaiian practitioners object to the tours outright, since manō are ʻaumakua.

species.name: Green sea turtle
species.note: Reliably seen on most wrecks; very large individuals on the YO-257.

species.name: Whitetip reef shark
species.note: Resting inside the San Pedro's portside overhang and around the YO-257. Unbaited, and entirely separate from the Haleiwa shark tours.

species.name: Sandbar shark
species.note: The common species on Haleiwa cage tours, which use bait. Encoded 'baited' for the cage product; the cage-free operator states it does not chum, so the same animal is encountered both ways on the same stretch of water. A genuine limitation of a single per-species field.

species.name: Galapagos shark
species.note: Same caveat as the sandbar shark.

species.name: Spotted eagle ray
species.note: Frequent around the Nashua tug.

species.name: Humpback whale
species.note: Dec-Apr. Acoustic only for divers, as at Kona: song is audible from 5-20 miles away on the deeper wrecks. In-water approach is federally regulated.

trip_formats.note: Two-tank boat mornings out of Honolulu and Waikiki to the south shore wrecks. Large operator market with a wide quality range and heavy cruise and resort traffic.
Shore entries exist but the wrecks that make Oahu worth diving are all boat access.

Format mismatch warning. The Haleiwa shark tours are the most heavily marketed in-water activity on Oahu and they are NOT diving: cage tours are snorkel from a surface cage, and the cage-free swims are open-water snorkelling with a safety diver. A certified diver searching 'Oahu shark diving' will be sold a surface product.

required_certs.note: The wreck cluster sits at 30-40m and is usually dived twice in a morning.
The Sea Tiger has open doors and hatches and is routinely entered.

conditions.experience_note: The wrecks are the gate, not the water. YO-257 and San Pedro sit around 30-38m and the Corsair at 33m, so this is deep recreational diving with short bottom times, and Advanced is the practical floor despite Oahu's easy reputation. Conditions themselves are benign on the south shore. The north shore is a different island in winter: Nov-Mar swell shuts down north-side diving entirely, which is why the shark tours cancel and the wreck diving does not.

operating_note: South shore wreck diving runs year-round and is sheltered. North shore is seasonal in practice: winter (Nov-Mar) brings the swell Oahu is famous for and the Haleiwa tours cancel frequently. Because the wrecks are unaffected, the destination reads 'open' throughout, with the north-side caveat carried in the trip formats.
